article_title: Social Skills Training (Early Childhood, Children with Disabilities)
citation: Social Skills Training. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report: Early Childhood Education Interventions for Children with Disabilities. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Behavioral social skills lesson pattern: instruct, model, practice, reinforce
description: The reviewed interventions share a recurring lesson structure: children are instructed on target behaviors, instructors model the behavior, children practice it with peers, and appropriate behavior is reinforced. In Guglielmo and Tryon (2001), "Instructors modeled the activities for the children using puppets and a short skit. Following this activity, children practiced the sharing skills with their peers," with reinforcement including continuous verbal acknowledgment and tangible rewards. LeBlanc and Matson (1995) similarly modeled with a puppet, had children model with a puppet and then with another child, and reinforced during a play phase.
requirements: Target behaviors must be specified (e.g., sharing, being in a group, greeting, initiating play)
Reinforcement of targeted behaviors during and after practice
constraints: In LeBlanc and Matson (1995), children engaging in inappropriate behavior were prompted toward an opposite positive behavior, with a one-minute time-out if they refused
target_learners: preschool children with disabilities or developmental delays
target_learning_goals: age-appropriate social skills such as sharing, joining a group, greeting, and initiating play
examples: Guglielmo and Tryon (2001) taught children to establish eye contact, tap children on the shoulder to gain attention, and ask to play with others
LeBlanc and Matson (1995) split each session into an approximately 15-minute instruction and modeling phase and an approximately 45-minute reinforced play phase
key_sources: Social Skills Training. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report: Early Childhood Education Interventions for Children with Disabilities. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/578

article_title: Repeated Reading
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2014). Repeated Reading: WWC Intervention Report, Students with Learning Disabilities. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Repeated reading as a flexible practice with seven variable implementation parameters
description: The report describes repeated reading not as a fixed protocol but as a practice whose implementation teachers can vary along seven parameters. As printed, "Teachers can vary" the criterion for progression to the next passage (minimum number of reads or a minimum reading rate of 85–100 words per minute), the instructional settings (teacher-directed, with same-age or cross-age peers, in groups, independently), the purpose, the materials (narrative texts, expository texts, poems, chants, songs, student- or class-written text), the modalities (silent with a tape, aloud with a model, choral, to a peer, to oneself), the length of the passage read, and the feedback provided on reading errors.
requirements: A teacher who selects passages and sets a progression criterion such as a minimum reading rate of 85–100 words per minute
constraints: The reviewed evidence covers individual delivery with a teacher in grades 5–12; the report does not rate effectiveness for the other configurations it lists
target_learners: students with learning disabilities in grades 5–12 with inadequate reading fluency
target_learning_goals: oral reading fluency
reading comprehension
examples: Settings range from teacher-directed one-on-one to work with same-age or cross-age peers, groups, or independent practice
Materials may include narrative texts, expository texts, poems, chants, songs, or text written by the student or class
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2014). Repeated Reading: WWC Intervention Report, Students with Learning Disabilities. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/576

article_title: Reading Recovery®
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, June). Reading Recovery® Intervention Report | English Language Arts Topic Area. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Reading Recovery training cascade: university-affiliated teacher training sites, teacher leaders, and certified teachers
description: Reading Recovery® sustains implementation through a three-level training infrastructure. Teacher training sites in public schools, affiliated with partnering universities, house teacher leaders who train teachers. Teacher leaders complete a yearlong training of graduate coursework and supervised practicums, and are expected to "provide initial training for up to 15 teacher candidates and provide ongoing support for 40 to 60 Reading Recovery® teachers or teachers in training annually." Teachers complete a yearlong graduate-credit training and must maintain registration by teaching at least eight students per year and participating in ongoing professional development.
requirements: Teacher leaders hold a master's degree and teaching credentials and complete a yearlong certification training
Teachers must be certified, experienced early elementary teachers and complete a year of training with graduate credit
Teachers must maintain registration by teaching at least eight students per year and attending ongoing professional development, typically no less than six sessions per school year
constraints: Neither contributing study provided details about the Reading Recovery® teacher training sites or the training of teacher leaders
Registration lapses after 1 year if teachers do not maintain the requirements
target_learners: Grade 1 students with low literacy achievement in districts implementing Reading Recovery®
target_learning_goals: Early literacy intervention delivered with training fidelity
examples: Based on survey results from one study, teacher leaders met 87% of the implementation standards, including attending 73% of training sessions and 98% of professional development sessions

article_title: eMINTS Comprehensive Program
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020). eMINTS Comprehensive Program Intervention Report │ Teacher Excellence Topic Area. NCEE WWC 2020-011. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Four-component design of eMINTS: sequenced professional development, coaching, technology integration, and online resources
description: The report enumerates four key components of eMINTS. Sequenced professional development delivers "approximately 140 hours of professional development focused on integrating technology into the classroom and developing lessons that use inquiry-based learning" over 2 or more years. Coaching provides one-on-one classroom sessions by instructional specialists plus group coaching to build school learning communities. Technology integration supports inquiry-based instruction, differentiated learning, and assessment. Online resources supply an eMINTS portal with assessments, lesson plans, example classroom websites, and online courses.
requirements: Trained instructional specialists to deliver professional development and coaching
Individual student access to Internet-connected computers or tablets for technology integration
constraints: A shorter version, eMINTS4All, includes fewer professional development sessions and coaching visits
target_learners: K–12 classroom teachers
target_learning_goals: Inquiry-based, technology-supported instruction
Classroom assessment and classroom management
Building a community of learning in schools
examples: At the end of the first year, teachers develop a classroom website with the help of the instructional specialist as a resource for students and their families
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020). eMINTS Comprehensive Program Intervention Report │ Teacher Excellence Topic Area. NCEE WWC 2020-011. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/705

article_title: Building Blocksâ"¢
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, December). Building Blocks. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Building Blocks multi-context implementation pattern: whole-group, small-group, centers, computer activities, and family letters
description: The curriculum distributes mathematics learning across several classroom contexts: whole-group instruction during circle time (approximately 5–15 minutes, four or five times per week), small-group instruction with 3 to 6 children (approximately 10–15 minutes, two or three times per week), hands-on center activities, and computer activities that "automatically adjust when children progress well or need additional help." Weekly family/caregiver letters describe the mathematics and home activities. This pattern lets teachers adapt activities to children's developmental levels while other children work independently.
requirements: Teachers used the Teacher’s Edition to locate relevant activities.
Teachers received 4–8 full days of initial training, monthly 2-hour refresher classes, and on-site coaching 1–2 times a month.
constraints: Center activities were mostly free-choice, so frequency and duration varied; the content and duration of professional development varied across the studies.
target_learners: preschool children
target_learning_goals: early mathematics knowledge aligned to learning trajectories
examples: In the three contributing studies, children in the comparison group were taught by teachers who did not participate in Building Blocks training and did not implement the Building Blocks sessions.

article_title: Really Great Reading's Foundational Literacy Programs
citation: Really Great Reading. (2023). Really Great Reading. https://www.reallygreatreading.com
title: Deliver foundational literacy instruction with existing classroom staff and no additional personnel
description: RGR is designed so that "Classroom teachers, paraprofessionals, or tutors can deliver instruction" and "No additional staff is required." This staffing model keeps implementation feasible within existing school resources, complementing the program's emphasis on efficient instruction and minimized teacher preparation time through digital lesson delivery tools.
requirements: Delivery by classroom teachers, paraprofessionals, or tutors already present in the school
target_learners: Early elementary students receiving Tier 1, Tier 2, or Tier 3 support
target_learning_goals: Foundational reading skills including phonics and fluency
examples: The studied implementation assigned instruction to regular classroom teachers across 13 schools

article_title: PAX Good Behavior Game — Reading
citation: Evidence for Learning. (2023). PAX Good Behavior Game (Evidence Rating). https://evidenceforlearning.org
title: Team-based group contingency for behavior management
description: The PAX Good Behavior Game organizes classroom behavior management around a group contingency: students are divided into two or more teams, and when a member violates class rules "discussed and agreed upon by the students themselves", the team receives a check mark. The team with the fewest checkmarks, or all teams meeting a set criterion, receives a small privilege such as lining up first for recess. This structure is "intended to create a situation in which students encourage and assist their peers to behave appropriately".
requirements: class rules discussed and agreed upon by the students themselves
teacher monitoring of student behavior
small privileges as reinforcers
target_learners: elementary school students
target_learning_goals: self-regulation and appropriate classroom behavior
examples: Teams receive checkmarks on a whiteboard for rule violations; the winning team or all qualifying teams receive a small privilege such as lining up first for recess.
key_sources: Evidence for Learning. (2023). PAX Good Behavior Game (Evidence Rating). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/pax-good-behavior-game-reading/

article_title: Corrective Reading — Elementary
citation: Corrective Reading. (2021). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/
title: Deliver Corrective Reading in small groups with sessions 4-5 days per week for optimal achievement gains
description: The article states the program "is most effective when taught in small groups" and that "Sessions should occur 4-5 days per week for optimal achievement gains". Delivery can occur inside or outside the regular classroom, and instructors may teach multiple groups across the school day.
requirements: Instructors may include general classroom teachers, special education teachers, intervention specialists, and paraprofessionals
constraints: The frequency recommendation reflects the article's stated conditions for optimal achievement gains, not a tested comparison in the summary
target_learners: Upper-elementary struggling readers in small intervention groups
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement gains
examples: Lesson delivery can occur within the regular classroom or outside of the regular classroom (pull-out).

article_title: Once Early-Reading Program
citation: Once Early-Reading Program: Evidence Rating Summary. (2025). https://once.org
title: Pair scripted tutoring delivered by non-specialist staff with weekly coaching based on session recordings and real-time progress data
description: The Once model makes non-specialist delivery viable by combining scripted, laptop-delivered lessons with a structured coaching loop: tutors receive weekly 30-minute coaching sessions from a consistent coach who reviews session recordings and provides targeted feedback, and a real-time data portal lets tutors, coaches, and administrators monitor student progress. This allows "staff without specialized reading instruction backgrounds to deliver sequenced lessons with fidelity". The article presents this staffing and supervision structure as integral to implementation.
requirements: A two-day, in-person training focused on the Science of Reading, the Once delivery method and model, and the Once technology, with ample time allocated for hands-on practice.
Weekly 30-minute coaching sessions from a consistent coach, plus laptop and internet access with a front-facing camera for session recording.
constraints: Coaching and data monitoring are described as components of the Once program specifically; the article does not report separate effects for the coaching component.
target_learners: PreK through first grade students receiving supplemental literacy tutoring
target_learning_goals: Early literacy skills delivered with fidelity by staff without specialized reading instruction backgrounds
examples: Tutors receive weekly 30-minute coaching sessions from a consistent Once coach who reviews session recordings and provides targeted feedback; a real-time data portal allows tutors, coaches, and administrators to monitor student progress.
key_sources: Once Early-Reading Program: Evidence Rating Summary. (2025). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/once-early-reading-program/

article_title: Building Assets Reducing Risks (BARR) — Attendance
citation: Building Assets Reducing Risks (BARR) program evidence summary. (2020). https://www.barrcenter.org
title: Sustain model implementation with multi-year sequenced professional development plus ongoing dedicated coaching
description: BARR pairs annual in-person training with continuous coaching: each school receives "two days of in-person professional development annually delivered through a sequenced, multi-year training plan," and "an average of more than 200 hours per year of personalized coaching and technical assistance." Year 1 training focuses on implementing the model; Years 2 and 3 address advanced topics such as effective team meetings, understanding trauma, reducing risky behaviors, and fostering student resilience.
requirements: A dedicated BARR coach assigned to each school providing structured weekly coaching sessions and quarterly on-site visits.
A sequenced, multi-year training plan using BARR materials and practice.
target_learners: teachers and school leaders implementing BARR
target_learning_goals: faithful implementation of the BARR model
continuous improvement and long-term sustainability
examples: BARR coordinators and administrators also join quarterly Professional Learning Community calls and attend the annual BARR National Conference.

article_title: Simple Solutions Learning – Standards-Based Math

article_title: I CAN Learn® Primary Mathematics

citation: Lenses on Literature. (2013). Lenses on Literature. https://www.literacydesigncollaborative.org
title: Sequenced literacy units organized around a Driving Task Prompt moving through comprehension, knowledge building, genre study, synthesis, and writing
description: This pattern organizes curriculum units and modules around a Driving Task Prompt within a disciplinary-literacy framework. Students explore complex, diverse texts through a sequenced instructional journey that includes comprehension, knowledge building, genre study, synthesis, and writing. The design purposefully builds knowledge and supports text-based analysis and communication across genres and formats.
requirements: Units require complex, diverse texts and standards-aligned rubrics for embedded formative assessment of performance tasks.
target_learners: middle school students
eighth-grade students
target_learning_goals: disciplinary literacy
text-based analysis
writing across genres and formats
examples: Teachers implemented at least two Lenses modules in history/social studies or science in the Kentucky study.
key_sources: Lenses on Literature. (2013). Lenses on Literature. https://www.literacydesigncollaborative.org

article_title: Lenses on Literature — Evidence for ESSA
citation: Lenses on Literature. (2013). Lenses on Literature. https://www.literacydesigncollaborative.org
title: Use a digital platform to deliver layered scaffolding, differentiation, and ongoing formative assessment with standards-aligned rubrics
description: Lenses is a hybrid program with print and digital components. The digital platform ensures that teachers can deliver layers of scaffolding and differentiation to meet varied learning needs, conduct ongoing formative assessment, and use standards-aligned rubrics to score periodic and summative performance tasks. The principle is that technology should serve differentiation and formative assessment within daily instruction.
requirements: A hybrid print and digital program structure with standards-aligned rubrics from the Stanford Center for Assessment, Learning, and Equity.
target_learners: middle school students
multilingual learners
target_learning_goals: differentiated literacy instruction
formative assessment of reading and writing
examples: The program provides robust scaffolds for multilingual learners and embedded formative assessments using standards-aligned rubrics.

article_title: EveryDay Intervention (Formerly InClass Today and EveryDay Labs)
citation: EveryDay Intervention (formerly InClassToday) Absence Reports Intervention — Evidence Summary. (2018). https://www.everydaylabs.com
title: Deliver personalized attendance information directly to parents as a low-burden absenteeism intervention
description: The article's program model is that mailing parents "actionable, personalized information about their student's attendance" can change attendance behavior without instructional changes at school. Implementation burden is minimal: staffing is "one district staff member to support program implementation (approximately 30 min/week)" plus a data staff member, with no professional development, training, or technology required.
requirements: Secure receipt of attendance data from the district
One district staff member (~30 min/week) and one district-level data staff member (< 3 hrs total)
constraints: No professional development or training required beyond the stated staffing; no technology required
target_learners: Students at risk of chronic absenteeism and their parents/guardians
target_learning_goals: Reducing absences so students attend and benefit from instruction
examples: In both randomized evaluations, at-risk students' families received mailed, personalized Absence Reports while control families did not.

article_title: Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System (EWIMS)
citation: Faria et al. (2017). Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System (EWIMS). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=early+warning+intervention+and+monitoring+system
title: Early warning monitoring cycle: identify at-risk students with attendance, behavior, and course performance indicators, intervene, and monitor progress
description: The pattern is a recurring school-level cycle in which a dedicated team uses routinely collected indicators — "engagement (attendance), behavior (suspension), and course performance (grades and credits)" — to flag students at risk of not graduating on time, assign them to interventions, and monitor their progress over time. The model is intended to help schools efficiently use data to both identify the at-risk population and provide targeted support.
requirements: A dedicated school team to lead and carry out the process
Data on attendance, suspensions, grades, and credits
target_learners: High school students in grades 9 and 10
target_learning_goals: Student persistence and progress in school
On-time graduation
examples: In the evaluation, EWIMS schools used the indicators to identify at-risk students and assign interventions, yielding lower chronic absenteeism than usual-practice schools.
key_sources: Faria et al. (2017). Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System (EWIMS). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=early+warning+intervention+and+monitoring+system

article_title: Chapter One (Formerly Innovations for Learning High Impact Tutoring)
citation: Chapter One. (2024). Chapter One — Evidence Rating: Strong. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org/chapter-one
title: Push-in short-burst tutoring with personalized dosage
description: The program's instructional pattern places tutors inside the regular classroom rather than pulling students out: tutors "work with individual students in 5-10 minute increment sessions during blocks of reading instruction or other opportune moments." Session length and frequency vary by student need and rate of progress, with students needing more support meeting daily for periods of time. A student-relay handoff minimizes interruptions to classroom instruction.
requirements: Part-time tutors embedded in the classroom who serve multiple classrooms across the school
target_learners: kindergarten and first grade students needing supplementary reading support
target_learning_goals: phonics
reading fluency
examples: Students making adequate progress meet with their tutor once or twice a week, whereas students identified as needing more support may meet daily for periods of time

article_title: Early Learning in Mathematics
citation: Early Learning in Mathematics (ELM): Evidence Rating. (2021). https://www.evidenceforessessments.org/early-learning-in-mathematics/
title: Focused coverage of a small number of key mathematical ideas with explicit, systematic instruction
description: ELM's instructional design pattern emphasizes depth over breadth: "The curriculum emphasizes a small number of key ideas in math to provide more focused coverage, instead of trying to teach a comprehensive but more surface set of skills." It pairs this focused coverage with "Explicit and systematic instructional design." The pattern structures a full year of 120 45-minute lessons plus daily calendar activities.
requirements: A full year of structured lessons (120 45-minute lessons plus daily 15-minute calendar activities) delivered by the classroom teacher.
constraints: The review does not isolate which design feature produced the effects; the pattern is described, not experimentally decomposed.

target_learning_goals: core early mathematics concepts and skills
examples: ELM implements this pattern through 120 45-minute lessons and daily 15-minute calendar activities for the whole class.

article_title: Galaxy Math
citation: Galaxy Math. (2013). Program description, Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org

description: Galaxy Math operationalizes tutoring as a scripted, fixed-dosage, one-to-one delivery model: "The program is scripted, and tutors are expected to follow the scripts without reading them or memorizing them." Sessions are "30-minute sessions 3 times a week for 16 weeks" delivered by paraprofessionals, standardizing implementation across tutors.

2-day initial workshop plus weekly coordinator meetings

article_title: PowerSchool Attendance Intervention
citation: PowerSchool Attendance Intervention. (2024). Evidence for ESI program review. https://www.evidenceforessi.org/
title: Automate personalization of family communication templates to reduce staff time burden
description: The review states that "[t]he ability to automatically populate a parent or student's name and real-time attendance data into communication templates greatly reduces the time burden for school staff." Attendance-communication tools should therefore pull names and live attendance data into message templates automatically, so educators can send accurate, personalized family messages at scale without manual entry.

target_learning_goals: Increasing family engagement and supporting student attendance
examples: The PowerSchool Attendance Intervention app auto-populates parent or student names and real-time attendance data into messaging templates used for two-way text and email communication with families.

article_title: Symphony Math
citation: Symphony Math. (2021). Symphony Math program description and evidence summary. https://www.symphonylearning.com
title: Require mastery of the current concept before advancing to the next in a sequenced math program
description: Symphony Math sequences mathematical concepts and does not let a student move on until the current concept is mastered. Because the time and practice students need is not uniform, the program lets students spend the time they need to master foundational concepts before progressing.
requirements: A sequenced progression of mathematical concepts with mastery assessment at each step
constraints: Requires allowing non-uniform amounts of time and practice per student
target_learners: K-8 students
target_learning_goals: Mastery of foundational mathematical concepts
examples: A student does not move to the next concept in the Symphony Math sequence until she has mastered the current concept

article_title: Symphony Math
citation: Symphony Math. (2021). Symphony Math program description and evidence summary. https://www.symphonylearning.com
title: Adaptive pacing that accelerates to locate need then slows until understanding is achieved
description: The program quickly moves students through the conceptual progression to identify their area of need, then slows progress until the necessary understanding has been achieved. This two-phase pacing pattern combines rapid diagnosis with remedial slowdown, and also alerts educators when students show signs of struggle.
requirements: A conceptual progression of skills and ongoing performance monitoring to detect the area of need
target_learners: K-8 students needing individualized math practice
target_learning_goals: Identifying and remediating individual areas of need in mathematics
examples: Once the area of need has been identified, the program slows the progress until the necessary understanding has been achieved

article_title: eMINTS
citation: eMINTS (enhancing Missouri's Instructional Networked Teaching Strategies): Program description and evidence summary. (2023). Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Build principal leadership and observation capacity alongside teacher professional development when implementing an instructional improvement program
description: eMINTS treats implementation leadership as part of the intervention itself: "The model also has a strong emphasis on helping principals understand and lead the program implementation and carry out teacher observations to support teachers' instructional performance." Professional development is thus directed not only at teachers but at principals and technology coordinators, so school leaders can understand, lead, and monitor the program rather than merely host it.
requirements: Principals receive professional development to understand and lead program implementation
Principals conduct teacher observations to support instructional performance
target_learners: principals
middle school teachers
target_learning_goals: program implementation leadership
instructional quality through observation and support
examples: Professional development is provided to principals, technology coordinators, and classroom teachers in middle schools.

article_title: Pirate Math
citation: Pirate Math. (2021). Evidence for Learning program summary. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au
title: Token reward with mapped milestone prizes sustaining engagement across tutoring sessions
description: Pirate Math embeds a motivational routine in its tutoring sessions: students receive gold coins for good work and place them on a treasure map. When they reach a picture of a treasure box, they earn a small prize. This recurring reward cycle structures motivation across the 16-week program.
requirements: A treasure map and small prizes must be available across the 16-week session sequence
target_learners: Third graders in remedial math tutoring
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and effort in tutoring sessions
examples: Students receive gold coins for good work, place them on a treasure map, and earn a small prize on reaching the treasure box picture.

article_title: Pirate Math
citation: Pirate Math. (2021). Evidence for Learning program summary. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au
title: Deliver supplemental math tutoring one-to-one outside ordinary math periods, staffed by teachers or trained paraprofessionals
description: Pirate Math delivers tutoring one-to-one, with tutors who may be teachers or paraprofessionals working with students outside of ordinary math periods. This staffing and scheduling model allows struggling third graders to receive intensive individual support without displacing their regular math instruction.

constraints: Requires scheduling sessions outside ordinary math periods, three per week over 16 weeks

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Zearn Math
citation: Zearn Math evidence review. (2024). https://zearn.org
title: Pair supplemental digital math programs with dedicated implementation support including professional development, coaching, and dosage monitoring
description: The review indicates that significant positive results occurred where Zearn Math was implemented with "accompanying professional development and coaching support for school leaders", which helps schools "establish dedicated time in the schedule for usage, build effective routines, and use data to ensure students reach the recommended dosage of three digital lessons per week". Support includes regular coach check-ins and motivational strategies such as classroom-based challenges to promote consistent lesson completion.
requirements: Dedicated scheduled time for program usage
Professional development and coaching for school leaders
Data-based progress monitoring toward the recommended dosage
Designated school or district points of contact for onboarding and rostering setup
constraints: The pilot implementation without full implementation support found no significant differences, suggesting support may be a boundary condition for effects.

target_learning_goals: Grade-level mathematics proficiency

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: OGAP Math Professional Learning System
citation: OGAP Math program description. (2024). Evidence for Learning. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org/ogap-math/
title: OGAP strand-based professional learning structure: cohorts of about 24 educators, four onsite days, and two follow-up coaching days
description: OGAP professional learning is organized by Strand, each aligned to a developmental progression in mathematics: Additive Reasoning (K–2), Multiplicative Reasoning (3–5), Fractional Reasoning (3–6), and Proportional Reasoning (6–8). Each strand is delivered to educator cohorts, often around 24 participants, through four onsite professional learning days, with districts able to space sessions several weeks apart. Two onsite follow-up coaching days, often during PLC time, "support transfer into classroom practice." Multiple strands may run simultaneously under the same structure.
requirements: Cohorts of about 24 educators per OGAP Strand
Four onsite professional learning days per strand
Two onsite follow-up coaching days, often scheduled during PLC time
constraints: Districts may choose consecutive sessions or a split schedule, with flexibility to space the sessions several weeks apart
target_learners: K–8 mathematics teachers participating in OGAP strands
target_learning_goals: Transfer of professional learning into classroom practice
Grade-band mathematical reasoning progressions (additive, multiplicative, fractional, proportional)
examples: Strands are aligned to grade-band progressions such as Multiplicative Reasoning (3–5) and Proportional Reasoning (6–8)

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Graspable Math — From Here to There (FH2T)
citation: From Here to There (FH2T): Program Description and Evaluation Evidence. (2023). https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au/the-toolkit/from-here-to-there/
title: Expression-transformation puzzle: match a starting expression to an equivalent target form via valid operations
description: The core design pattern of FH2T is a transformation puzzle: "The program presents a starting expression and a mathematically equivalent target expression. Students manipulate the original expression to match the target form." Because moves must be "mathematically valid operations," students practice algebraic manipulation by direct interaction with notation rather than by answering discrete items. The pattern embeds practice of distribution, factoring, inverse operations, and order of operations inside the game's goal structure.
requirements: A starting expression paired with a mathematically equivalent target expression
An interface allowing students to drag and transform expressions using mathematically valid operations
constraints: Applied in the article to algebraic expressions and equation solving for introductory prealgebra/algebra
target_learners: Middle and high school students learning introductory prealgebra or algebra
target_learning_goals: Fluency with algebraic manipulation operations, including distribution, factoring, inverse operations, and order of operations
examples: FH2T tasks ask students to transform a given expression into a target form using operations such as distribution and factoring.

Adaptivity operates within games, between games, and across the system to give "a customized pathway between skills based on prior performance," with cohesive narrative and interactive characters supporting engagement.

constraints: Designed for pre-kindergarten through second grade number sense and operations content

description: The curriculum organizes word-recognition instruction into "three developmental levels of progression in word recognition: simple alphabetic (SIPPS Beginning Level), spelling-pattern (SIPPS Extension Level), and polysyllabic/morphemic (SIPPS Challenge Level)." A separate variant, SIPPS Plus, covers the simple alphabetic and spelling-pattern phases but is designed specifically for older students in grades 4–12, allowing the same progression to serve adolescent struggling readers.

target_learning_goals: Progression from simple alphabetic to spelling-pattern to polysyllabic/morphemic word recognition

citation: SIPPS program description and outcomes review. (2022). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/
title: Use placement and embedded mastery tests to drive grouping, pacing, and reteaching decisions
description: The article describes an assessment system in which "Assessment data determines placement in the program" and flexible groups based on placement results provide differentiated instruction. Criterion-referenced mastery tests embedded at designated intervals document mastery of phonics and high-frequency words and "support instructional decisions to guide reteaching, which may include adjusting pacing and delivery." This keeps instruction matched to individual progress through an accelerative scope and sequence.

target_learners: K-12 students in differentiated small groups within a foundational reading program
target_learning_goals: Efficient progression through foundational reading skills matched to individual need

article_title: Reading Edge

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org

description: In JUMP Math, "Math concepts are reduced to increasingly smaller steps until students achieve mastery, then built back up incrementally to meet the curriculum demands." Students receive extensive practice at each step. This stepwise reduction-and-rebuild structure is the core instructional mechanism of the program's guided-discovery approach.

target_learning_goals: mastering math concepts and meeting curriculum demands

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org
title: Use ongoing assessment to ensure comprehension before moving to new material
description: JUMP Math treats assessment as continuous: "Assessment is ongoing and considered essential to ensure comprehension before moving on to new material." This gates progression on demonstrated understanding rather than fixed pacing, complementing the program's stepwise mastery structure and individual pacing within a shared class concept.

description: JUMP Math uses "a range of models (concrete materials, tables, diagrams) ... strategically to help students grasp abstract concepts but the models are removed as soon as students are able to work without these supports." article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction (ECRI)

Professional development workbooks and a Leadership Guide

science materials kit and trade books accompanying the lessons

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use

description: The brief's first key recommendation is that districts should "Develop a culture of data use among all levels of staff." The recommendation is one of four the brief offers to districts building data-use capacity.

The recommendation ties data analysis directly to district improvement goals.

title: Secure and dedicate resources to conduct analyses and interpret findings

The recommendation is drawn from the brief's work with districts in strategic data use initiatives.

article_title: Scaling Programs with Research Evidence and Effectiveness (SPREE)
citation: Nan Maxwell, Scott Richman. (2019). Scaling Programs with Research Evidence and Effectiveness (SPREE). The Foundation Review, vol. 11, issue 3. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use the SPREE process to identify and provide the support grantees need to demonstrate effectiveness and build scaling conditions
description: The article recommends that funders use the SPREE process to diagnose what grantees need. It states the process "can also help funders identify and provide the kind of support grantees need in demonstrating that an intervention is effective and in building the conditions needed to scale it successfully." This makes grantee support a deliberate funder activity rather than an afterthought.

article_title: Challenges in Adolescent Reading Intervention: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial

title: Schedule adolescent reading interventions so students do not miss grade-level content
description: This principle holds that pull-out intervention arrangements for adolescent struggling readers should be designed so that students do not sacrifice access to grade-level coursework. The Oakland LLI trial found that "Students who were pulled out of other classes to receive LLI were particularly negatively affected, possibly as a result of missing grade-level content." Scheduling is therefore a design lever, not just a logistical detail.

constraints: The article frames the missing-content explanation as possible, not established

mastery of grade-level English language arts/literacy standards
examples: In the Oakland trial, some students were pulled out of other classes to receive LLI, and this subgroup showed particularly negative outcomes

citation: Kate Place, Kara Conroy, Gregory Chojnacki. (2023). A Road Map for Building Evidence that Drives Learning and Improvement. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Engage the community in focus as collaborators throughout all phases of research and design
description: Evidence-based innovation should begin by identifying a need, problem, or challenge together with the community whose goals should drive design. article_title: Conducting Implementation Research in Impact Studies of Education Interventions: A Guide for Researchers
citation: Hill, C. J., Scher, L., Haimson, J., & Granito, K. (2023). Conducting Implementation Research in Impact Studies of Education Interventions: A Guide for Researchers. title: Conduct implementation analyses within impact studies so educators can judge local fit
description: The guide's rationale is that implementation analyses conducted as part of impact studies serve adoption decisions: they 'can help educators know whether a tested intervention is likely to be a good fit for their own settings'. Because impacts alone do not reveal what delivery conditions produced them, embedding implementation research gives practitioners the information needed to judge transferability to their contexts.
requirements: Impact studies should incorporate implementation analyses for their findings to inform local adoption decisions.

target_learning_goals: Judge whether an evidence-based intervention fits a local setting
examples: The guide was written to help researchers design and conduct these kinds of analyses within impact studies.

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1)
citation: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Treat evidence building as iterative learning that may loop back or abandon a solution
description: The checklist's activities focus on iterative learning rather than a one-way march through phases. Teams may complete a phase multiple times, move backwards to a previous phase, or abandon a solution altogether based on what they learn. This principle frames evidence building as a cyclical design process in which findings at any phase can send teams back to earlier design work.
requirements: Teams must be willing to revisit or repeat phases based on evidence gathered
constraints: Iteration may mean abandoning a solution altogether
target_learners: students in a priority community
target_learning_goals: designing and refining solutions through iterative evidence building
examples: The checklist explicitly states that iterative learning may mean completing a phase multiple times or moving backwards to a previous phase

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1)
citation: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Ground solution design in a well-defined theory of change developed with the priority community
description: Phase 1 of the evidence-building process directs users to develop a solution based on a well-defined theory of change for how that solution is expected to improve outcomes for students or teachers in a priority community. The design work is done in collaboration with stakeholders from that community, so the causal logic connecting the solution to outcomes is explicit before refinement and testing begin.

constraints: The theory of change is specific to outcomes for students or teachers in the identified priority community

teachers

description: The report organizes state apprenticeship system capacity around an enumerated set of characteristics, spanning program registration, employer recruitment, apprentice diversity, rural and opioid-related expansion, financial incentives, costs and federal grants, COVID-19 impacts, and data infrastructure. article_title: Comparing the Reliability and Predictive Power of Child, Teacher, and Guardian Reports of Noncognitive Skills
citation: Shuaizhang Feng, Yujie Han, James J. Heckman, Tim Kautz. (2022). Comparing the Reliability and Predictive Power of Child, Teacher, and Guardian Reports of Noncognitive Skills. The Proceedings of the National Academy Sciences, vol. 119, issue 6. https://www.pnas.org
title: Collect teacher reports when a single perspective on children's noncognitive skills must suffice
description: Because collecting ratings from multiple perspectives about a single child is costly and the article finds child and guardian reports add minimal predictive power beyond teacher reports, programs needing one perspective should rely on teacher reports. The article states "teacher reports have the highest internal consistency and are the most predictive of children's later cognitive outcomes and behavior in school." This applies to program evaluation and monitoring school systems.
requirements: A teacher who knows the child must be available to provide the rating.
constraints: Collecting data from multiple perspectives is costly, and the article notes there is limited evidence on the benefits of this approach.

target_learning_goals: measurement of noncognitive or socioemotional skills such as persistence and self-control
examples: The study compared child, guardian, and teacher reports in a longitudinal survey for program evaluation and school-system monitoring purposes.

article_title: Megastudies Improve the Impact of Applied Behavioural Science
citation: Kautz, T., Milkman, K. L., Gromet, D., et al. as printed in full author line. (2021). Megastudies Improve the Impact of Applied Behavioural Science. Nature, vol. 600. https://www.nature.com
title: Test many intervention ideas at once in a shared population and outcome to improve the evidentiary value of behavioural science
description: The article recommends running many interventions concurrently in the same population on the same objectively measured outcome for the same duration, because typical scattered studies lack comparability. Because "Forecasts by impartial judges failed to predict which interventions would be most effective," the authors argue this "underscor[es] the value of testing many ideas at once and, therefore, the potential for megastudies to improve the evidentiary value of behavioural science."
requirements: A large shared population, an objectively measured outcome held constant across arms, a fixed duration, and multiple independent teams designing interventions.
constraints: In the demonstrated megastudy, only 8% of interventions produced behaviour change significant and measurable after the four-week intervention, so parallel testing does not guarantee durable effects.
target_learners: Adults targeted by applied behavioural-science interventions, here fitness-chain members
target_learning_goals: Identifying which behaviour-change interventions work, e.g. increasing physical exercise
examples: 30 scientists from 15 different US universities worked in small independent teams to design 54 different four-week digital programmes encouraging exercise, all compared on the same gym-attendance outcome.

Activities are planned with templates and tools, and cohort learning is complemented by project scoping, provider matching, and thought partnership, as implemented in the CBSL pilot with nine K-12 education grantees.

examples: The partnership articulated this criterion when defining what strong equity-centered strategic learning looks like in the CBSL initiative

article_title: Implementing Covid-19 Routine Testing in K-12 Schools: Lessons and Recommendations from Pilot Sites
citation: Divya Vohra, Patricia Rowan, John Hotchkiss, Kenneth Lim, Aimee Lansdale, So O'Neil. (2021). Implementing Covid-19 Routine Testing in K-12 Schools: Lessons and Recommendations from Pilot Sites. Mathematica Research & Evaluation.
title: Build community engagement and stakeholder buy-in, supported by effective communication and simplified informed consent, to sustain school testing programs
description: The report's implementation lessons hold that testing programs succeed when schools invest in community engagement and buy-in from key stakeholders. It states that "Community engagement and buy-in from key stakeholders are critical to the success of a testing program," and that "Effective communication and simplified informed consent processes can a long way in building trust in testing programs and boosting participation rates." Effective communication with the school community
Simplified informed consent processes

citation: Herrmann, M., Clark, M., James-Burdumy, S., Tuttle, C., Kautz, T., Knechtel, V., Dotter, D., Smither Wulsin, C., & Deke, J. (2019). title: Do not assume intensive principal professional development focused on structured observation and targeted feedback will change leadership practice or raise achievement without direct evidence
description: This principle captures the study's central lesson: an intensive program "focused primarily on helping principals conduct structured observations of teachers' classroom instruction and provide targeted feedback" was implemented as planned yet produced no intended changes in principal practice and no achievement gains. Designers and funders of principal professional development should treat observation-and-feedback training as unproven at scale and plan for rigorous evaluation, since teacher-reported support even moved in the opposite direction.

target_learning_goals: Instructional leadership practices: conducting structured classroom observations and providing targeted feedback to teachers
examples: The study randomly assigned 100 elementary schools, half to receive the program, and compared student achievement and teachers' perceptions of principals' practices across groups.

title: Use Bayesian methods to make factorial experiments with many treatment arms feasible when studying complex interventions
description: The article recommends Bayesian methods as a tool for researchers studying complex interventions, because they make factorial experiments with many treatment arms vastly more feasible. As the authors conclude, "Bayesian methods are a valuable tool for researchers interested in studying complex interventions. They make factorial experiments with many treatment arms vastly more feasible." The recommendation rests on the simulation evidence of lower MDEs under hierarchical priors and partial pooling.

target_learning_goals: designing adequately powered experiments to test multiple factors and factor levels

title: Use Bayesian methods to make factorial experiments with many treatment arms feasible in education research
description: The paper recommends that researchers interested in studying complex interventions adopt Bayesian analysis for factorial designs. Because traditional inference "may require prohibitively large sample sizes to perform complex factorial experiments," Bayesian methods with hierarchical priors and partial pooling make "factorial experiments with many treatment arms vastly more feasible," enabling testing of multiple implementation factors such as dosages and implementation strategies and their interactions.
requirements: A research question involving a large set of related interventions or implementation factors suited to a factorial design
constraints: The feasibility advantage is demonstrated for complex experiments with many factors and factor levels
target_learners: Education researchers
target_learning_goals: Designing efficient experiments that test multiple factors and interactions
examples: Power calculations for a U.S. Department of Education experiment showed Bayesian designs reaching a given MDE with roughly half the sample size needed classically for 72 treatment arms

article_title: Rolling Back Zero Tolerance: The Effect of Discipline Policy Reform on Suspension Usage and Student Outcomes
citation: Johanna Lacoe, Matthew P. Steinberg. (2018). Rolling Back Zero Tolerance: The Effect of Discipline Policy Reform on Suspension Usage and Student Outcomes. Peabody Journal of Education, vol. 93, issue 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/rolling-back-zero-tolerance-the-effect-of-discipline-policy-reform-on-suspension-usage-and-student-outcomes
title: Policymakers should weigh suspension-usage and student-outcome consequences when designing district-level discipline reforms
description: The article's stated purpose is that its findings "should inform policymakers and practitioners on the implications of district-level reforms for suspension usage and the potential consequences for student outcomes." Districts revising zero-tolerance policies toward "more tempered disciplinary responses" should anticipate that limiting suspensions for nonviolent misconduct may not reduce total suspensions and may coincide with increased serious incidents, truancy, and achievement decline.

target_learning_goals: Student attendance and academic achievement in math and English language arts
examples: Philadelphia's 2012-2013 reform limited suspensions for nonviolent student misconduct and granted principals greater discretion over more serious misconduct.

citation: Naihobe Gonzalez. (2017). Small Changes Make a Big Difference: How Behavioral Science Improved Participation in Advanced Placement (Issue Brief). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Use personalized messages added to existing communications to encourage student participation in advanced coursework
description: The brief presents personalized messages as a low-cost behavioral-science nudge: a small change in how information is presented—a personalized message added to a test score report—can substantially change students' decisions to participate in a program. It reports that "Personalized messages can be a cost-effective way to encourage students," grounded in the finding that message recipients were 49 percentage points more likely to participate in AP classes.

target_learning_goals: increasing participation in advanced coursework and AP exam taking

article_title: The Evidence Base for How We Learn: Supporting Students’ Social, Emotional, and Academic Development
citation: Stephanie M. Jones, Jennifer Kahn. (2017). The Evidence Base for How We Learn: Supporting Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development. Washington, DC: The Aspen Institute, National Commission on Social, Emotional, and Academic Development. https://www.aspeninstitute.org
title: Educate the whole child by integrating social, emotional, and academic development
description: The principle holds that schooling should support students' social, emotional, and academic development together rather than separately, because success is "inextricably linked to healthy social and emotional development." The consensus statement presents this as the evidence base for how we learn, framing belonging, purpose, collaboration, goal-setting, and perseverance as working alongside literacy, numeracy, and scientific knowledge.

constraints: The available text asserts the evidence base without printing the underlying studies, so implementation should rest on the full consensus statement.

academic achievement
workforce life skills
examples: The Council of Distinguished Scientists issued consensus statements of evidence for the National Commission on Social, Emotional, and Academic Development, published by the Aspen Institute in 2017.

article_title: Understanding Types of Evidence: A Guide for Educators
citation: Gregory Chojnacki, Alexandra Resch, Alma Vigil, Ignacio Martinez, Steve Bates. (2016). Understanding Types of Evidence: A Guide for Educators. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: When choosing technologies, base decisions on evidence about which options are effective
description: The guide recommends that educators making technology decisions ground their choices in effectiveness evidence rather than in marketing claims alone. It states: "When making decisions about which technologies to use, you need evidence about which options are effective to make the best possible use of your technology budget." The guide then equips educators to judge evidence quality by describing its four evidence types.
requirements: Access to information sources containing evidence about the effectiveness of the technology options under consideration
constraints: Framed for decisions about which technologies to use and how to allocate a technology budget
target_learners: educators making technology adoption decisions
target_learning_goals: making evidence-informed technology purchasing decisions
examples: The guide orders its four evidence types from weakest to strongest and pairs each with examples of information sources, so readers can locate stronger evidence for effectiveness claims

citation: Emilyn Ruble Whitesell. (2016). A Day at the Museum: The Impact of Field Trips on Middle School Science Achievement. title: Schools can provide enrichment experiences such as field trips without sacrificing student test scores
description: This principle holds that enrichment experiences like field trips are compatible with, rather than in tension with, academic accountability pressures. The study's evidence indicates field trips "can contribute positively to student achievement," so shifting resources toward them need not depress standardized test performance. It is grounded in a quasi-experimental analysis of New York City eighth-grade science exam outcomes.

constraints: Effects were estimated for middle school students in New York City on a standardized eighth-grade science exam

target_learning_goals: science achievement on standardized assessments

citation: Brian Gill, Joshua Furgeson, Hanley Chiang, Bing-Ru Teh, Joshua Haimson, Natalya Verbitsky-Savitz. (2016). title: Match causal estimands when using within-study comparisons to validate nonexperimental methods
description: The article states, citing Cook, Shadish, and Wong (2008), that "WSCs require that the experimental and nonexperimental methods assess the same causal estimand." This principle guides the design of replication studies: before judging whether a nonexperimental method replicates an experimental result, researchers must ensure both approaches target the same quantity. The article operationalizes this by comparing to ITT estimates under noncompliance.
requirements: Researchers must identify and align the causal estimand of the experimental and nonexperimental analyses before conducting a replication comparison
constraints: Under control-group noncompliance, standard approaches diverge in estimand, requiring an ITT-based comparison rather than CACE

examples: The article's own WSC compared nonexperimental estimates to the experimental ITT estimate to satisfy the same-estimand requirement

title: Use measures of academic behaviors and mindsets, alongside test scores, to inform teacher development and evaluation policy
description: The paper positions its findings as directly usable for policy: because teachers affect behaviors and mindsets substantially and differently from test scores, "Findings can inform policy around teacher development and evaluation." The principle is that teacher development and evaluation systems should attend to non-tested outcomes and the practices that develop them, not only test scores. It rests on the paper's findings about teacher effects and their dissociation from test-score effectiveness.

constraints: The evidence base is upper-elementary teachers and math outcomes, as reported in the paper's summary.

target_learning_goals: academic behaviors in class

happiness in class
examples: The paper reports that teachers effective at improving behaviors and mindsets often are not the same as those who raise math test scores, motivating evaluation systems that capture both.

citation: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2015). Re-Imagining Accountability in K-12 Education: A Behavioral Science Perspective. Working Paper 39, Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Design school accountability regimes with multiple forms of accountability, multiple measures, and feedback mechanisms
description: The paper's central design recommendation is that an effective accountability regime for schools should combine several elements rather than rely on test-based sanctions alone. It concludes that effective accountability "will involve (1) multiple forms of accountability, (2) multiple measures of educational practice and educational outcomes, and (3) feedback mechanisms to promote the improvement of practice." This multi-pronged structure is offered as the design implication of the behavioral science literature reviewed in the paper.

constraints: Grounded in the behavioral literature as interpreted by the authors; the available text prints no empirical test of the combined design

target_learning_goals: Improving school performance and educational practice through better-designed accountability
examples: The paper's conclusion specifies the three-part structure: multiple forms, multiple measures of practice and outcomes, and feedback mechanisms to improve practice

title: When constructing teacher value-added models, include student and peer background characteristics, especially for districts with many disadvantaged students
description: The article recommends attention to control-variable choice because specification differences have direct implications for which teacher estimates change. It reports that "teachers in a district with a large fraction of disadvantaged students receive lower ratings when background characteristics are omitted," so omitting background controls disadvantages such teachers. The principle applies to policymakers and analysts constructing VAMs.
requirements: Value-added models must isolate teachers' contributions to student achievement to be valid, which requires decisions about student and peer control variables and lagged achievement scores.
constraints: The article notes other modeling choices have smaller practical consequences, and none are as important as selecting which assessment to use as the outcome measure.

target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of teachers' contributions to student achievement

The checklists function as a reusable reporting pattern that researchers apply when drafting or reviewing methods sections.

constraints: The guide addresses reporting of measures in education research reports, not study design itself

target_learning_goals: complete and transparent reporting of measures in education research
