article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Researchers should take time to understand a digital learning platform's learning environment and capabilities before planning research within it
description: The report's first consideration holds that researchers must conduct due diligence on a DLP before planning studies, because research must fit within learning environments that already exist. Researchers should inquire about the learning setting, theory of action, typical implementation, and available content, since "researchers will need to be prepared to explore, modify, and study their ideas within learning environments that already exist." This saves the expense of building a platform while requiring creativity in fitting research interests to it.
requirements: Time investment in an information-gathering stage to determine alignment between research interests and the platform's learning opportunities
constraints: Researchers may need to be more innovative or creative in conceptualizing how their research interests fit within an existing environment rather than building new tools
target_learners: Education researchers considering studies within digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Aligning research questions with platform learning opportunities and capabilities
examples: SEERNet offers a Guide to Doing Research on DLPs, and the AIMS Collaboratory is creating a searchable catalog of researcher-ready DLPs covering grade level, content area, and type of research supported
key_sources: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210

article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Explore existing platform data before fully specifying a research plan to inform questions, design, and sample selection
description: The report advises that DLPs offer access to data on large numbers of users or full user populations, usable for secondary analysis or to refine hypotheses and run power calculations. The stated consideration is "taking time to explore this available data before fully specifying a research plan," because existing data reveal available data structures and user behavior and help relate a planned experimental contrast to current platform activity.
requirements: Access to existing datasets on platform users, or prior-study data providing context on sample sizes and dependent measures
constraints: The depth of existing data varies across platforms; some data may only support school-level covariates rather than individual demographics
target_learners: Education researchers planning studies in DLPs
target_learning_goals: Designing feasible, well-powered studies grounded in real platform data
examples: Platforms may offer data from similar prior studies that provide context on sample sizes and statistics on built-in dependent measures for power calculations
key_sources: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210

article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Collaborate with the DLP team to align planned experimental comparisons with platform capabilities and constraints
description: The report's third consideration is that researchers should hold ongoing conversations with the platform team, since interventions must fit existing content and structure. Researchers "may need to refine their interventions/planned comparisons based on DLP capabilities and other limitations," and must learn what content can be created or modified. Higher-customization studies may require active recruitment or additional consent processes rather than drawing on the full user base.
requirements: Frequent collaboration between researcher and DLP team, especially during initial planning stages
constraints: Some platform content components cannot be modified or manipulated; studies with high customization may require the researcher to actively recruit participants
target_learners: Education researchers designing experimental comparisons within DLPs
target_learning_goals: Designing experimental contrasts that are feasible within platform constraints
examples: Researchers need to understand limits on the type of content that can be created or modified for experimental designs and the reasons for those limitations
key_sources: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210

article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Weigh the tradeoffs of readily accessible DLP data against the effort of integrating additional data sources
description: The report's fourth consideration addresses data availability: DLPs may lack individual demographic data while collecting school-level covariates such as locale type or Title I status. Researchers should "weigh the tradeoffs and level of effort that may be required to access and integrate additional data," possibly through data sharing agreements, embedded surveys, or LMS/SIS roster linking, and may iterate toward richer data across multiple small-scale studies.
requirements: Understanding whether missing data reflects technical constraints that could be relaxed or is so by design; appropriate permissions and data privacy processes for linking external data
constraints: A DLP may not have access to individual student or teacher demographic data without connecting to other data sources or embedding a survey
target_learners: Education researchers conducting studies in DLPs
target_learning_goals: Obtaining the outcome, demographic, and contextual data needed to answer research questions
examples: Some platforms coordinate data privacy by de-identifying district-provided demographic data so the researcher never sees personally identifiable information
key_sources: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210

article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Leverage DLP process data on user behavior to address analytic questions and measure intermediate outcomes
description: The report urges researchers to use the robust log data DLPs generate, such as which tasks students begin, time spent, and detailed progress. Such data can reveal attrition or compliance indirectly and "may serve as a measure of important intermediate outcomes, or mediators, that are often very difficult to collect in conventional research settings." Researchers unfamiliar with log data should work with platform teams and review codebooks and data dictionaries.
requirements: Working with the platform team to understand how users interact with the system to generate the desired log data; reviewing codebooks and data dictionaries from prior studies
constraints: Researchers are not always provided direct information on attrition or compliance; platforms vary in ability to create or add instruments for more distal outcomes
target_learners: Education researchers, particularly those trained in conventional classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Measuring engagement, progress, and mediating processes during learning
examples: Time stamps of activities such as reading a prompt or attempting to solve a problem allow identifying students who stopped participating or skipped certain materials
key_sources: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210

citation: Judi Fusco, Pati Ruiz, Jeremy Roschelle. (2023). Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning. Digital Promise presentation. https://tech.ed.gov/ai/
title: Design educational AI as intelligence augmentation that centers educators' professional judgment and learners' voice

In its 2021 blog post it states: we recommend a focus on Intelligence Augmentation in education that would put educators' professional judgement and learners' voice at the center of innovative designs and features. This positions AI as supporting, not replacing, human decision-making in teaching and learning.

educators

article_title: Realizing District-Community Driven Outcomes Through Inclusive Innovation
citation: White, L. P. and Merritt Johnson, A. (2024, May). Realizing District-Community Driven Outcomes Through Inclusive Innovation. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/214
title: Four conditions Core Teams identified as supporting solution success: the Inclusive Innovation model structure, student voice, safe spaces, and flexible implementation
description: Across the pilot districts, Core Team members identified four conditions that enabled their co-created solutions to achieve intended outcomes. The report states that "these four themes—Inclusive Innovation, student voice, the creation of safe spaces, and flexible implementation—were instrumental in creating the conditions that enabled the solution to achieve its intended outcomes." Student voice meant students were involved from design through implementation and decision-making; safe spaces encouraged open participation, particularly for students of color; flexibility allowed adjustments based on classroom or community needs, emphasizing teacher and student choice.
requirements: Students involved from the beginning of solution development, not only implementation
Environments where students can share perspectives among adults who traditionally hold power
constraints: Conditions were identified retrospectively by participants in four pilot districts, not experimentally tested
target_learners: secondary students
district and community Core Team participants
target_learning_goals: co-designing equity-centered solutions to locally identified educational challenges
examples: In Pilot District 3, teachers adapted the Compact Writing Assignments to fit classroom dynamics, which a student said made them "work better for the classes now"

article_title: Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are
citation: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Four dimensions for reaching all learners: level, pacing, voice and choice, and supports
description: The paper organizes personalized learning practice around four dimensions that address learner variability. Level means adjusting tasks to the most productive difficulty, drawing on game-design calibration; pacing means mastery-based progression; voice and choice means extended experiences where students select or modify topics and products; supports means tailoring academic, college and career planning, and family supports. As the paper states, "Four dimensions that address learner variability are discussed below: Level Pacing Voice and Choice Supports."
requirements: Requires teachers and tools able to differentiate tasks, assess mastery frequently, and offer structured choices
constraints: The paper describes these dimensions as design commitments for personalized environments, not as tested interventions
target_learners: K-12 students in diverse classrooms, including learners with disabilities, English language learners, and gifted learners
target_learning_goals: Mastering content and skills at productive levels of challenge; developing learner agency and ownership
examples: Adaptive systems such as DreamBox, i-Ready, Istation, and A2I calibrate work automatically; Challenge Based Learning connects student projects to real-world challenges; advisory systems provide a sustained adult relationship at the secondary level
key_sources: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org
grain_size: lesson/unit-level organization of personalized learning environments

article_title: Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are
citation: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Challenge Based Learning framework: three phases with key design elements
description: The paper describes Challenge Based Learning as connecting student projects to real-world challenges, divided into three interconnected phases: Engage, Investigate, and Act. It lists key elements including that everyone is a learner, learning moves beyond the classroom walls, challenges are learner-inspired and owned, there is space and freedom to fail, technology is authentically used, and learners continuously reflect. As printed: "The CBL Framework is divided into three interconnected phases – Engage, Investigate, and Act."
requirements: Community involvement beyond the classroom; ubiquitous access to information and technology; intentional slowing for critical and creative thinking; documentation and reflection throughout
constraints: Described as a framework with design elements; the paper reports no comparative effectiveness data for it
target_learners: K-12 students working on collaborative real-world challenges with teachers, families, and community members
target_learning_goals: Deep subject area knowledge and skills for thriving in an ever-changing world, including collaboration and creative problem solving
examples: The framework's elements include a safe space to fail, receive feedback and try again, with iteration built into all phases
key_sources: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org

article_title: Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are
citation: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Hold high expectations for all learners so personalization advances equity rather than tracking
description: The paper argues personalized learning can advance equity only when paired with high expectations, contrasting it with traditional tracking that became permanent with different expectations and outcomes per group. It states that "Personalized learning has the potential to help advance equity in schools, as long as expectations are held high for all." To avoid permanent low tracks, personalized learning schools frequently remix performance groups, mixing academically homogeneous with heterogeneous groupings.
requirements: Clearly stated high expectations for everyone; equitable opportunities in the line of sight for all; remixing of performance groups rather than fixed tracks
constraints: Equity advocates worry about the shift of control back to states under ESSA; students most harmed by traditional systems include students of color, first-generation college students, economically disadvantaged students, and English language learners
target_learners: All students, particularly vulnerable groups harmed by traditional tracking
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to college- and career-ready outcomes
examples: Wilusz and Templeton's five elements of personalized learning that can lead to more equitable outcomes, including common standards for all students and choice in designing content, pathways, and products
key_sources: Barbara Pape and Tom Vander Ark. (2020). Policies and Practices That Meet Learners Where They Are. Digital Promise Global. https://global.digitalpromise.org

article_title: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market
citation: Amber Laxton, Mike Berlin, Patti Constantakis, Ph.D. (2017). Accelerating Change: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Offer flexible pricing and licensing models — seat transfer, concurrent use, and pay-by-usage — because the adult learner population is constantly in flux
description: The guide recommends that entrepreneurs adopt hassle-free, flexible purchasing and licensing models as a core value proposition for learning providers. Because the adult learner market is constantly in flux, providers look for arrangements allowing reuse and transfer of seats among students, concurrent-use software, or pay-by-usage, especially during low enrollment. Flexibility should also extend to how and where tools are used, with learners able to access tools from their own devices wherever they are. The guide also advises offering group discounts to consortia and bundling professional development and ongoing support, citing a Digital Promise report that training and support is key to successful technology implementations.
requirements: Every tool should be designed to be easy to use without training, with professional development and ongoing support provided alongside it
constraints: The guide states entrepreneurs in education face a lengthy sales cycle even in adult learning, so licensing clarity and affordability matter
target_learners: adult learning providers such as community colleges, K-12 districts, libraries, and correctional institutions
target_learning_goals: expanding access to adult basic education and job-skills technology under constrained budgets
examples: The guide's Getting Started section instructs entrepreneurs to create hassle-free purchasing models that allow seat transfer and pay-by-usage where enrollment might be low
key_sources: Amber Laxton, Mike Berlin, Patti Constantakis, Ph.D. (2017). Accelerating Change: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/36eceee2-6442-4c5c-8fa1-7b9e7eab4533

article_title: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market
citation: Amber Laxton, Mike Berlin, Patti Constantakis, Ph.D. (2017). Accelerating Change: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Contextualize instruction by integrating reading, math, and digital literacy into industry-specific training for workforce segments
description: The guide identifies contextualized instruction as the most critical value driver for employers and workforce channels, so that employees gain skills directly related to their industry and professional goals. It states that integrating reading, math, and digital literacy into industry-specific training is proving to be quite effective, citing examples such as airline mechanic courses that teach literacy and math through real job problems and home healthcare workers taking mobile ESL classes to communicate with doctors. Entrepreneurs serving this segment should ensure content is contextualized to a work environment or learners' daily lives.
requirements: Content must map to the specific industry and professional goals of the employing organizations
constraints: The guide's support is practitioner testimony and program examples rather than controlled evidence of effectiveness
target_learners: low-wage and frontline workers
adult learners in employer and workforce training programs
target_learning_goals: job-related basic skills: literacy, math, digital literacy, and ESL in work contexts
career advancement and middle-skill role readiness
examples: Savannah Technical College offers airline mechanic training integrating literacy and math where those skills solve real problems on the job; Cell-Ed delivers mobile ESL to Los Angeles home healthcare workers
key_sources: Amber Laxton, Mike Berlin, Patti Constantakis, Ph.D. (2017). Accelerating Change: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/36eceee2-6442-4c5c-8fa1-7b9e7eab4533

article_title: Rapid Cycle Pilots: Using Edtech to Support English Learners
citation: Luke, Christina C.; Gibson, Sierra; Francisco, Aubrey T. (2017). Rapid Cycle Pilots: Using Edtech to Support English Learners. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Include comparison groups in edtech pilots whenever possible to generate interpretable efficacy results
description: This principle holds that pilot studies of edtech products should include a comparison group of students not using the tool so that outcome differences can be attributed to the tool. The article's two pilots illustrate the contrast: Cajon Valley's comparison-group design supported a significant finding, while Vista's single-group design left results uninterpretable. As the report states, districts' results "demonstrate the necessity to include comparison groups when possible in pilots in order to generate powerful results."
requirements: A pool of comparable students not using the tool, matched or at least comparable to pilot students, available for the same pre- and post-assessments
constraints: The article notes Cajon Valley's comparison group was constrained to fifth grade, limiting the analysis to that grade level
target_learners: K-12 English Learners in district edtech pilots
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether an edtech tool improves English language development and reading outcomes
examples: Cajon Valley included a comparison group and could attribute Lexile differences to Achieve3000; Vista had no comparison group, so the authors state it is possible non-users grew substantially or declined, and no conclusions could be drawn
key_sources: Luke, Christina C.; Gibson, Sierra; Francisco, Aubrey T. (2017). Rapid Cycle Pilots: Using Edtech to Support English Learners. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/383e02ba-587a-4192-be68-175543798661

article_title: Delivering on the Promise of Digital Equity
citation: Weaver, D'Andre J., Ph.D. (2022). Delivering on the Promise of Digital Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Close digital divides by engaging underrepresented communities in planning rather than paving over their interests, as interstate highway construction did
description: Drawing an analogy to the 1956 Interstate Highway Act, whose planners "physically paved over and uprooted established Black and poorer communities," the report argues today's digital infrastructure planners must instead plan with and learn from underrepresented communities and act on what is heard. It states that "the requirements of the new digital equity grant programs, the moral choice, and the pathway to finding the best solutions all lead to engaging and coordinating with these communities in new and significant ways," ensuring community ideas, interests, and needs manifest in state implementation strategies.
requirements: State planners must devote time, effort, and money to engagement and coordination with communities and the municipalities and nonprofits that serve them
constraints: The report cautions this engagement "is essential to success—not a grant obligation that simply needs to be met"
target_learners: students and families in historically and systematically excluded communities
target_learning_goals: equitable digital access, skills, and use for full participation in society and the economy
examples: Lindsay Unified's year-long community engagement effort with more than 200 parents in 2006-07 produced the district vision for 24/7 access to learning that anchored its digital equity transformation
key_sources: Weaver, D'Andre J., Ph.D. (2022). Delivering on the Promise of Digital Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/38939984-18ea-4af0-8081-c787ac30d48d

article_title: An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects
citation: Noakes, S., Shell, A., Murillo, A., Van Nostrand, P., Ruiz, P., Cornick, S., and Karim, S. (2024, October). An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/232
title: Center educators' and students' voices throughout the AI research and development process through co-design and collaboration
description: This principle holds that successful, equitable AI-enabled educational tools require deliberate collaboration with end users. The report states it is crucial to establish meaningful relationships with educators and students, "ensuring their voices are central throughout the research and development (R&D) process," so developers gain insight into authentic needs and priorities. Cohort projects such as EdLight's family co-design and KIPP Chicago's teacher co-design exemplify this approach, using sandbox environments and small-scale testing to gather feedback and iterate.
requirements: Meaningful relationships with educators and students established early in R&D
Sandbox environments for safe exploration and small-scale testing to gather feedback
target_learners: K-12 students
K-12 educators and families
target_learning_goals: Development of equitable AI-enabled educational tools that address authentic classroom needs
examples: EdLight co-designed a platform with families based on surveys, focus groups, and empathy interviews
KIPP Chicago developed AI-powered tools through the co-design efforts of its teachers
key_sources: Noakes, S., Shell, A., Murillo, A., Van Nostrand, P., Ruiz, P., Cornick, S., and Karim, S. (2024, October). An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/232

article_title: An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects
citation: Noakes, S., Shell, A., Murillo, A., Van Nostrand, P., Ruiz, P., Cornick, S., and Karim, S. (2024, October). An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/232
title: Build educator AI literacy through professional learning that explains how AI is trained, fine tuned, and functions, equitably distributed across districts
description: The report recommends professional learning focused generally on AI literacy rather than only on operating a specific tool. Educators need to understand which tools incorporate AI, what the tools use AI to do, and how AI is trained and fine tuned, so they can continually evaluate the accuracy of AI-generated content. The report stresses that AI literacy support "needs to be equitably distributed among educators," with high-quality professional learning accessible regardless of the zip code in which teachers work.
requirements: Professional learning that covers how AI is trained and fine tuned and how it functions
Equitable distribution of AI literacy support across all districts

Belonging

article_title: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning
citation: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning. (2015). Digital Promise Global, Making Learning Personal for All series. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Four categories of factors influencing learner variability
description: The article organizes research on learner variability into four categories of factors: content area skills, social and emotional skills, cognitive skills, and background, environment, and experiences. It stresses that "while each of these categories individually affects learning, no single factor acts independently" and that understanding how the factors combine is critical. The pattern frames Learner Models and personalization decisions: a struggling decoder, for example, must also be understood through working memory. It calls for continued research on combinations of factors.
requirements: Research must continue into how these factors affect learning in various combinations
constraints: Current research is described as insufficient on how factors interact; no single factor acts independently
target_learners: All K-12 learners, given the growing diversity of U.S. classrooms
target_learning_goals: Improving the accuracy and precision of personalization across academic, cognitive, and social-emotional domains
examples: The article illustrates the pattern with decoding supported by multisensory strategies when working memory is low

article_title: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning
citation: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning. (2015). Digital Promise Global, Making Learning Personal for All series. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Ground personalized learning in learning sciences research on learner variability
description: The article argues that because personalization can only be as good as what is known about learners, the education community must leverage research on how students learn to "improve the accuracy and precision of personalization." It criticizes emerging definitions of personalized learning for omitting "the explicit acknowledgement of the importance of learning sciences research" and calls for translational research determining which approaches work for which students in what context. Technology should make this research accessible and usable at scale.
requirements: Access to research on learner variability; translational research on which approaches work for which students in which contexts
constraints: Not all personalization approaches, materials, and products are effective with all students in every situation
target_learners: All learners, including the growing diversity of U.S. public school students
target_learning_goals: Effective, equitable personalization of objectives, approaches, content, pace, and tools
examples: The article cites the Cooney Center/New America market scan showing most popular literacy apps reference no research, and proposes technology tools such as the Research Map to make research accessible

article_title: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning
citation: Research and the Promise of Personalized Learning. (2015). Digital Promise Global, Making Learning Personal for All series. https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Inclusive design and assistive technologies benefit all learners (curb-cut effect)
description: Drawing on inclusive design and Universal Design for Learning research, the article states that "most assistive technologies and inclusive design approaches also help all learners learn more effectively." Jutta Treviranus is quoted asserting that designing for accessibility is just better design, illustrated by the curb-cut effect: sidewalk curb cuts designed for wheelchairs ended up benefiting people pushing strollers and riding bikes. Products designed for learners with impairments affecting vision, speech, or writing can also help learners struggling with literacy or numeracy more broadly.

constraints: The article presents this via cited research and expert assertion, not as a tested result of its own

target_learning_goals: Effective literacy and numeracy learning supported by accessible product design
examples: Assistive products for vision, speech, or writing impairments that also help other learners with literacy or numeracy struggles; the curb-cut analogy from sidewalk design

article_title: Rapid Cycle Pilots: Improving Ed-Tech Products through Feedback

title: Run small, targeted pilots confined to one grade level or subject area to identify suitable ed-tech products

title: Authentic co-design is not rushed or forced, and there is untapped knowledge everywhere in school communities.

article_title: Operation Outbreak: Exploring the Affordances and Challenges of Experiential Simulations in Education for Scalability
citation: Kelly McNeil, Sharin Jacob, Quinn Burke, and Stefani Pautz Stephenson. (2026). Operation Outbreak: Exploring the Affordances and Challenges of Experiential Simulations in Education for Scalability. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Implementation grains for simulations: single lesson, multi-week unit, and schoolwide event, with larger doses producing deeper learning when well-supported
description: The review organizes simulation integration into three time-based "grains": single-lesson simulations that are "the easiest to slot into a traditional schedule" but yield modest depth; multi-week units allowing students to "return to the simulation, test new ideas, and build on previous discoveries"; and schoolwide events like Operation Outbreak that are highly engaging but low-feasibility without strong support. The review concludes that "even small doses of simulation gameplay can be beneficial, but larger doses (time-span and scale) tend to produce deeper learning provided they are well-supported." Educators are advised to weigh feasibility against desired impact.
requirements: Single-lesson grains need clear, narrow learning goals and a brief debrief; multi-week units need curricular integration and ongoing assessment; schoolwide events need administrative approval, cross-subject coordination, and follow-up classroom activities.
constraints: Schoolwide events are typically rare without strong support and may be one-time annual events; the review notes students may remember the excitement more than the academic lessons without integrated reflection.
target_learners: K-12 students
career and technical education (CTE) students
target_learning_goals: subject-matter content knowledge
systems thinking
scientific inquiry and problem-solving
engagement and motivation
examples: The review cites River City implemented over about two weeks and EcoMUVE over multiple class sessions as multi-week grains, and Operation Outbreak as a schoolwide day-long or multi-day event grain.

article_title: Strategic Surprise and the Future of Educational R&D
citation: Uncapher, M. & Roschelle, J. (2025, November). Strategic surprise and the future of educational R&D. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/277
title: Make solvable, high-leverage problems the organizing unit of education R&D
description: The paper recommends shifting from field-initiated to problem-focused research: invest in the discipline of problem definition, replace generic goals such as improving literacy with measurable, time-bound challenges, involve practitioners in all research stages through co-design, and build infrastructure for cumulative progress. A ripe problem is one where concerted effort could produce measurable change in the near term, with lessons that generalize.
requirements: Requires tolerating risk and failure in pursuit of breakthroughs with outsized impact, enabling bold bets that may fail but offer disproportionate upside.
constraints: The paper warns that if educational research responds to surprise only through normative, paradigmatic studies, transformative potential may not be harnessed.
target_learners: Education researchers and the practitioners who co-define research problems with them
target_learning_goals: Directing research effort toward timely, solvable challenges that drive systemic value
examples: The paper's researchers recommendation tells investigators to move beyond what interests them to what moves the needle, defining problems actionable within cycles.

article_title: Continuing the educator micro-credential movement
citation: Center for Teaching Quality (CTQ) and Digital Promise. (2017). Continuing the educator micro-credential movement. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Successful micro-credential implementations share careful messaging, broad buy-in, and educator-led learning systems
description: The report states that "the most successful micro-credential implementations to date are marked by a few key characteristics, including careful messaging around the purpose and value of micro-credentials and the buy-in across a school or district, from classroom educators to administrators." Districts, states, and unions are urged to "build a system of educator-led learning — virtual and face-to-face — that guides how micro-credentials are earned," with new roles for professional development providers, district managers, and university faculty. The report calls clear communication of goals from the start, plus supports throughout, the most important condition for success.
requirements: Communicating clearly about the goals of a micro-credential effort from the get-go and providing the right supports throughout the process
target_learners: K-12 educators, administrators, and district and state professional learning leaders
target_learning_goals: Earning micro-credentials as competency-based professional learning and leadership development
examples: Baltimore County educators worked with school-based instructional coaches on micro-credentials aligned with district priorities; Charlottesville structured its pilot for novice educators and mentors through its Learning Management System
key_sources: Center for Teaching Quality (CTQ) and Digital Promise. (2017). Continuing the educator micro-credential movement. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials

article_title: Continuing the educator micro-credential movement
citation: Center for Teaching Quality (CTQ) and Digital Promise. (2017). Continuing the educator micro-credential movement. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Make micro-credentials feasible by taking something off teachers' plates rather than adding them on top of existing professional development
description: The report argues micro-credentials "cannot just be dropped on top of the existing system of traditional, workshop-oriented professional development." Educators need dedicated time to develop and practice competencies and to collect and submit evidence, which has implications for district structures such as professional development and professional learning communities. A Charleston County teacher who completed a CTQ micro-credential on collective leadership is quoted: "It is very important for us to take something off teachers' plates. We cannot just add this without subtracting something else." The report adds that the new system must be reflected in formal policies such as teacher contracts and collective bargaining agreements.
requirements: District structures such as professional development time and professional learning communities must provide time for developing, practicing, and evidencing competencies
constraints: The report notes, citing National Board research, that teachers in high-need schools, because of lack of administrative support and adequate time, are less likely to participate in the National Board Certification process — so working conditions can make a significant difference in engagement
target_learners: K-12 classroom educators, especially those in high-need schools
target_learning_goals: Engaging in competency-based professional learning through micro-credentials
examples: Early adopters CTQ worked with in South Carolina and Tennessee were enthusiastic but wondered what would be taken off their plates so they could fully engage

article_title: Unveiling the Value of Exploration: Insights from NSF-Funded Research on Emerging Technologies for Teaching and Learning
citation: Prado, Y.; Ouyang, S.; Risha, Z.; Ferguson, C.; Gardner, S.; Mallavarapu A.; Kelley, C.; Martin, W.; Glazer, K.; Hampton, S.; Fusco, J.; Pillai, S.; Walker, E.; Roschelle, J. (2024). Unveiling the Value of Exploration: Insights from NSF-Funded Research on Emerging Technologies for Teaching and Learning [Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/230
title: Five recurring innovation themes in NSF EXP project outcomes: accessibility, alternative CS modalities, VR/AR for STEM and workforce, broadening participation, and educator-centered AI
description: Qualitative analysis of 51 Project Information Pages submitted by RETTL PIs yielded recurring themes of project innovations. These include "Expanding accessibility for learners through digital tools," such as the SAIL 2 project's gamified virtual reality with signing avatars for ASL learning; alternative modalities in CS education using AI, AR/VR, tangible computing, and interdisciplinary learning; VR/AR tools for STEM education and workforce development; broadening participation of marginalized groups through technology; and centering educators in AI/ML tools so teachers remain at the forefront of decision making. Co-design with youths and LLM limitations and successes were cross-cutting themes discussed within the others.

constraints: Themes derive from 51 pages submitted by RETTL PIs, a self-selected subset of the portfolio

STEM concept understanding
critical data literacy

article_title: Transfer for Future Learning of Fractions within Cignition’s Microtutoring Approach
citation: Roschelle, J., Cheng, B. H., Hodkowski, N., Haldar, L., & Neisler, J. (2020). Transfer for future learning of fractions within Cignition's microtutoring approach [Project Report]. Digital Promise. http://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12265/95
title: Three-part TFL task structure: elicit prior knowledge, bridge with instruction, assess transfer
description: Each TFL task follows a three-part structure. Portion A elicits relevant prior knowledge and provides information on whether students are ready for transfer. Portion B provides bridging instruction between the source and target of transfer. Portion C assesses whether the student can use prior knowledge in the new way. The authors found this structure strengthened measurement quality by revealing whether weak performance stemmed from missing conceptual foundations or weak transfer.
requirements: Requires a tutor or instructor who can deliver the bridging instruction in Portion B
Requires prior knowledge tasks that successfully elicit the source concepts
constraints: Task delivery depends on the tutoring environment's ability to support needed representations
target_learners: fifth-grade students learning fractions
target_learning_goals: transfer of fraction concepts to division and generalization
examples: The three-part structure did not change during seven iterations of the Fraction Division task and four iterations of the Fraction Generalization task.

article_title: AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218
title: Teach AI literacy practices without AI tools, particularly in the early grades
description: The report recommends that AI literacy skill development begin offline: 'each of these practices can be learned and/or taught without the use of an AI tool.' The authors 'suggest that learners should explicitly engage in AI literacy skill development (such as analyzing and organizing datasets) without AI tools, particularly in the early grades,' so that foundational practices are built before learners apply them to AI tools.
requirements: Educators identify offline analogues for each AI literacy practice, such as analyzing and organizing datasets without AI tools
constraints: Recommended particularly for early grades
target_learners: early grades K–12 learners
elementary educators
target_learning_goals: foundational AI literacy practices such as data analysis and algorithmic thinking
examples: The report suggests analyzing and organizing datasets as an offline AI literacy activity for young learners

article_title: AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218
title: Explain how AI works mechanistically, not through metaphors like human-like intelligence
description: The report recommends that explanations of what AI is and how it works 'not be couched in metaphors like "human-like" or examples of AI's powers, but rather be a mechanistic discussion.' Key points should cover how AI uses data, that models rely on statistics and identifying key features of data, and that generative systems synthesize new content by predicting outputs such as the next word or pixel. Explanations may be pitched at many levels of detail depending on the audience.
requirements: Explanations should cover how AI uses data, that models rely on statistics, and how GenAI predicts outputs such as the next word or pixel
constraints: Level of detail should be adapted to the audience
target_learners: K–12 learners
educators
school leaders
target_learning_goals: understand how AI systems work mechanistically
examples: The report provides a three-step explanation adapted from MIT Media Lab and MIT STEP Lab: obtaining and curating data, training a model, and using the model to receive outputs

title: Avoid anthropomorphizing AI: refer to AI as it and avoid calling GenAI errors hallucinations
description: Because computers cannot take into account context and emotions, lack consciousness, and are 'not reflective or able to assess its actions,' the report states 'we caution against anthropomorphizing AI.' The authors remind users 'that AI tools should be referred to as "it" rather than pronouns and avoid referencing GenAI errors as "hallucinations" to avoid making light of mental health issues (Ruiz & Glazer, 2024).' This supports the Core Value of Centering Human Judgment by keeping the distinction between human and machine capabilities clear.
requirements: Educators and users maintain the human-machine distinction in language when discussing AI tools with learners
target_learners: K–12 learners
educators
school leaders
target_learning_goals: center human judgment when using AI
understand limits of AI capabilities
examples: The report cites Ruiz & Glazer (2024) for the recommendation to avoid the term hallucinations

title: Non-linear AI literacy learning journey cycling through Understand, Evaluate, and Use
description: The report illustrates the framework in action through a high school lesson on AI chatbots, 'following a winding pathway of the three Modes of Engagement.' Students first learn how chatbots work, then responsibly tinker with prompting while noting questions, research those questions with evidence, center human judgment through Socratic seminar discussion, center justice through an Ethics Matrix of stakeholders and values, and optionally design a chatbot for a community problem. The report states 'engagement in AI literacy is non-linear and intertwined, where each mode of engagement builds and strengthens on each other to foster overall AI literacy.'

constraints: Illustrated for a high school audience

target_learning_goals: understand how AI chatbots work
evaluate chatbot outputs and design for bias and transparency
use AI chatbots responsibly and creatively
examples: The lesson uses an Ethics Matrix (building off MIT RAISE) where students identify stakeholders invested in AI chatbots and the values of each stakeholder

article_title: Tough As Nails and Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia
citation: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs
title: Ground research and education design in civic imagination because people cannot work toward a future they cannot see
description: Drawing on Jenkins and Shresthova's civic imagination rationale, the presentation holds that inclusive research must help communities envision futures before pursuing them. Its first rationale states: "People can't work toward a future if they can't see it first", illustrated by contrasting circa-1993 career horizons (teacher, miner, nurse) with emerging regional possibilities such as entrepreneurship, eco-tourism, agtech, and computing careers.
requirements: Research and pathway design must surface and make visible plausible future careers and identities for the community
constraints: Framed for communities like coal-transitioning Appalachia where prior career horizons were narrow
target_learners: K-8 students and their teachers in Eastern Kentucky
target_learning_goals: Envisioning future educational and career possibilities
Civic imagination
examples: Slides contrast circa-1993 career options with 2023-and-beyond options including computing, eco-tourism, and agtech

article_title: Tough As Nails and Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia
citation: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs
title: Include community members in designing futures they will inhabit, since people do not want to design a future they are not in
description: The presentation's second civic imagination rationale is that design processes must include the people whose future is at stake: "People don't want to design a future that they aren't in." It illustrates this with a teacher's reflection after local industry presenters (Appalachian Wireless) connected to students: the presenters conveyed that "the skills they use/need are the exact skills I see in my students", producing what the teacher called a big "A-ha" moment.
requirements: Local industry and community voices must be present in curriculum design and professional learning
constraints: Grounded in Appalachian community contexts where outside-designed futures are distrusted
target_learners: Teachers and district leaders designing K-8 instruction
target_learning_goals: Connecting student skills to authentic local career applications
examples: Appalachian Wireless employees presented at a summer institute, prompting teachers to see student skills mirrored in local tech careers

citation: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs
title: Foster a sense of agency and permission so learners feel entitled to help shape their community's future
description: The third civic imagination rationale holds that "People need to feel a sense of agency or permission to help shape that future." The presentation links this to community cultural wealth: district leaders aimed to improve students' aspirational, linguistic, navigational, and resistant capital while building on rich familial (kinship) and social capital, per their KySTE 2023 presentation. A Summer 2022 teacher reflected: "I want to encourage my students to be innovative and proud of their region."
requirements: Educational design must affirm existing cultural wealth (kinship, social capital) while growing aspirational and navigational capital
constraints: Stated for Appalachian communities characterized by kinship, love of place, egalitarianism, and independence

target_learning_goals: Aspirational capital
Innovation identity
Regional pride
examples: A Summer 2022 teacher survey respondent reported the week was eye opening and resolved to encourage student innovation and regional pride

citation: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs
title: Apply rigor in inclusive research by taking community preconditions seriously when identifying interventions worth studying
description: The presentation proposes a definition of rigor for community-engaged research that treats inclusion as exactness rather than softness. It argues research that helps people work toward futures requires inclusion, and that "rigor (strictness, exactness, rigidity) in our research is applied in taking these preconditions seriously (when identifying the interventions worth studying), and in the studying." This reframes methodological strictness as inseparable from who defines the problems studied.
requirements: Research problem selection must be governed by the community's own preconditions (visibility of futures, inclusion, agency)
constraints: Articulated for partnership-based design research in a specific regional context
target_learners: Educational researchers and district partners
target_learning_goals: Designing rigorous, community-grounded research studies
examples: The RPP identifies interventions worth studying only after establishing the civic imagination preconditions with district partners

article_title: Teacher’s Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning
citation: Judi Fusco, Sarah DiMaria, Beverly Yeadon, Linette Victor, Sarah Hampton, Janet Kolodner, London Jenks, Susan Yoon. (2024). Teacher's Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Use an asset-based approach to classroom culture to balance status relationships and help students feel valued
description: Drawing on Bielaczyc and colleagues (2013) and Webb (2009), the primer recommends fostering a safe, supportive classroom culture by helping each student recognize the strengths and assets they bring to collaboration. As the primer explains, "an asset-based approach that highlights how each student plays an important role during collaboration helps balance status relationships among students by raising awareness of the multiple skills needed to accomplish the group task." Teachers should frequently discuss the importance of multiple abilities, comment on contributions of students who may be perceived as less important, and emphasize that no one person is best at every ability. The goal is a place where students feel valued and comfortable taking risks and sharing ideas.
requirements: Teachers must discuss the importance of multiple abilities and stress that all students bring important skills
constraints: The primer ties this to establishing trust through strong teacher-student relationships, which research links to engagement, attendance, grades, and lower dropout rates
target_learners: K-12 students in collaborative groups, including students perceived as less important to their groups
target_learning_goals: Willingness to take risks, share ideas, and work together during collaborative learning
examples: The primer cites Webb (2009) on teachers discussing multiple abilities and commenting on contributions of students perceived as less important to the group
key_sources: Judi Fusco, Sarah DiMaria, Beverly Yeadon, Linette Victor, Sarah Hampton, Janet Kolodner, London Jenks, Susan Yoon. (2024). Teacher's Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/6dc71c9f-b523-4c36-9da8-d98b364e17e0

article_title: Teacher’s Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning
citation: Judi Fusco, Sarah DiMaria, Beverly Yeadon, Linette Victor, Sarah Hampton, Janet Kolodner, London Jenks, Susan Yoon. (2024). Teacher's Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Act as a facilitator during collaboration: guide rather than direct, monitor groups, and intervene only when necessary
description: The primer's central during-collaboration principle is that collaborative learning works best when teachers act as facilitators. As the primer summarizes the research, "collaborative learning works best in classrooms where teachers act as facilitators: guiding rather than directing, empowering students, and using effective intervention techniques to support student learning." Teachers should stand back, let students interact, listen, and intervene when necessary — for example when a group is stalled, enmeshed in a misconception, or one student is dominating. Intervention is best done by asking questions to open up discussion. Teachers can use rubrics or checklists to monitor group climate, collaborative skills, and learning without feeling overwhelmed.
requirements: Well-structured tasks and clear expectations so students can sustain discussions without continuous teacher presence
constraints: The primer notes productive struggle is a key part of learning, but teachers must judge when struggle is too much and plan how to guide students toward the goal
target_learners: K-12 STEM students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: Sustaining meaningful peer discussion, self-regulation, and deeper content learning during group work
examples: The primer lists intervention situations including a stalled group, unanswerable questions, shared misconceptions, unresolvable disagreements, and a dominating student, with example teacher prompts for each

article_title: Scaling Up Design of Inquiry Environments
citation: Roschelle, J., Mazziotti, C. & Means, B. (2021). Scaling Up Design of Inquiry Environments. In C. Chinn & R.G. Duncan et al (Eds.), International Handbook on Learning and Inquiry. Routledge. ISBN 9781138922600. https://isbnsearch.org/isbn/9781138922600
title: Five complementary strategies for scaling inquiry environments: understand context, engage expertise, build a coherent system, work with practitioners, measure and iterate
description: From reflections on six scaled inquiry environments (including SimCalc, GLOBE, LASER, WISE, River City, and Building Blocks), the chapter distills five strategies: "Through our review of each team’s reflections on these cases, we identified five useful scaling strategies. We see these as complementary strategies, not alternatives." The strategies are understanding the context and niche, engaging a breadth of expertise, developing a coherent learning activity system aligning curriculum, technology, professional development, and assessment, working with practitioners through co-design and partnerships, and measuring and iterating with aligned learning measures and implementation indicators.

target_learning_goals: Inquiry learning outcomes sustained at scale across diverse settings
examples: The GLOBE program mapped its curriculum onto accountability standards and developed GLOBE books for early readers to win school-schedule time

article_title: A New Narrative: How Unlocking the Power of R&D Through Inclusive Innovation Can Transform Education
citation: Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2024). A New Narrative: How Unlocking the Power of R&D Through Inclusive Innovation Can Transform Education. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Collective Ownership requires side-by-side collaboration and intentional power distribution with communities
description: Collective Ownership recognizes that "creating effective education solutions requires side-by-side collaboration with the students, parents, families, and communities that education is meant to serve." It requires people with traditional power to embody humility that enables intentional distribution of power across the entire team, creating conditions that invite team members to lead, contribute, and take risks. The article's four R&D principles include committing to a shared understanding of collective leadership, developing a shared vision, creating a plan to co-lead implementation, and establishing shared approaches to support and sustain solutions. Superintendents must be listeners and learners with the capacity to sit back and let others lead.
requirements: District leaders must cede traditional hierarchical power and adopt listening and learning postures
Teams must establish mutually agreed-upon processes, decision-making structures, and continuous improvement cycles
target_learners: students, families, and communities historically excluded from education decision-making
target_learning_goals: equitable solution design
community ownership of education innovation
shared leadership capacity
examples: Three Pennsylvania districts (Avonworth, Hampton Township, South Fayette) supported teachers of color to design and lead Teaching is My Favorite Color, with superintendents explicitly stepping back to let teachers lead

citation: Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2024). A New Narrative: How Unlocking the Power of R&D Through Inclusive Innovation Can Transform Education. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Student Voice and Leadership tenet: students as prioritized collaborators in education R&D
description: The Student Voice and Leadership tenet holds that "students are collaborators and their perspectives are prioritized in the creation of solutions to educational challenges." Four R&D principles operationalize this: center the voices and leadership of students proximate to the challenge, commit to disrupting power dynamics, co-create engaging student-friendly structures and processes with students, and value and validate student lived experience in problem definition and solution design. The work starts with teaching adults that students can and should lead R&D efforts to dismantle inequities, rather than involving students later to advance adult perspectives.
requirements: Adults must learn to listen and champion students' rightful place in R&D with actions signaling the primacy of student voice
Structures and processes must be accessible and designed for student-first engagement
Students' choices must carry greater weight in decision-making processes
target_learners: students proximate to educational challenges, especially from historically marginalized communities
target_learning_goals: student agency
student engagement
equitable solution design
examples: Bristol Township students received weighted votes on solutions and PD design; Sunnyside student interns conducted research and designed three solutions for writing engagement
