article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Modify the classroom learning environment to decrease problem behavior
description: Many effective classroom-focused interventions alter or remove factors that trigger problem behavior, which can result from a mismatch between the classroom setting or academic demands and a student's strengths, preferences, or skills. The guide states that "Teachers can reduce the occurrence of inappropriate behavior by revisiting and reinforcing classroom behavioral expectations; rear-ranging the classroom environment, schedule, or learning activities to meet students' needs", and by adapting instruction to promote high rates of engagement and on-task behavior. This recommendation carries the panel's strong evidence rating.
requirements: Revisit, re-practice, and reinforce classroom behavior expectations
Modify the classroom environment to encourage instructional momentum
Adapt or vary instructional strategies to increase opportunities for academic success and engagement
constraints: Carrying out reward-based practices must fit students' age and developmental stage, since different forms of motivation are appropriate to different developmental stages
target_learners: Elementary general education students (K-5)
target_learning_goals: Increased student engagement and on-task behavior; decreased inappropriate behavior
examples: The guide suggests proactive classwide and individual strategies such as a change in instructional groupings, the seating plan, or the order or pace of reading and math instruction once teachers understand their classroom's behavioral hot spots.
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/4

article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Teach and reinforce new skills to increase appropriate behavior and preserve a positive classroom climate
description: Just as explicit instruction can remediate academic skill deficits, it can teach students the social and behavioral skills they are expected to exhibit at school. Teachers should actively teach socially and behaviorally appropriate replacement skills to individual students and the whole class, so that "teachers help students with behavior problems learn how, when, and where to use these new skills", and should manage consequences so reinforcers follow appropriate behavior and are withheld for inappropriate behavior. This recommendation carries the panel's strong evidence rating.
requirements: Identify where the student needs explicit instruction for appropriate behavior
Teach skills by providing examples, practice, and feedback
Manage consequences so that reinforcers are provided for appropriate behavior and withheld for inappropriate behavior
constraints: Acquiring positive behaviors takes time; the guide notes challenging behaviors are learned over a long period and progress monitoring with celebration of small achievements helps sustain effort
target_learners: Elementary general education students (K-5) with behavior skill deficits
target_learning_goals: Socially and behaviorally appropriate replacement behaviors and adaptive skills
examples: The guide frames the parallel with academics: some students' failure to meet behavioral expectations reflects deficits in specific social or behavioral skills, addressed through explicit instruction and consistent positive reinforcement.
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/4

article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Draw on relationships with professional colleagues and students' families for continued guidance and support
description: Social relationships and collaborative opportunities play a critical role in supporting teachers managing disruptive behavior. The guide recommends that teachers treat "parents, school personnel, and behavioral experts as allies who can provide new insights, strategies, and support" when addressing individual students' behavior problems, collaborating with other teachers, building partnerships with school, district, and community behavior experts, and encouraging families to participate as active partners in teaching and reinforcing appropriate behavior. This recommendation carries a moderate evidence rating.
requirements: Collaborate with other teachers for continued guidance and support
Build collaborative partnerships with school, district, and community behavior experts when problems warrant help from outside the classroom
Encourage parents and other family members to participate as active partners
constraints: When behavior problems warrant behavioral or mental health professionals, teachers are encouraged to ensure services address classroom behavior issues directly
target_learners: Elementary students whose behavior problems warrant support beyond the classroom teacher
target_learning_goals: Reducing individual students' problem behavior through coordinated school and home support
examples: The overview notes schools with strong, trusting staff relationships are more likely to have teachers willing to engage in new practices and consequently help produce gains in student outcomes, citing Bryk and Schneider (2002).
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/4

article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Assess whether schoolwide behavior problems warrant adopting schoolwide strategies or programs, and if so, implement ones shown to reduce negative and foster positive interactions
description: A teacher may be more successful creating a positive classroom behavioral environment when schoolwide efforts also exist. Classroom teachers, in coordination with administrators, grade-level teams, and special educators, should involve a school improvement team, collect information on behavioral hot spots throughout the school, monitor implementation and outcomes with efficient data collection, and, if warranted, "adopt a packaged intervention program that fits well with identi-fied behavior problem(s) and the school context". This recommendation carries a moderate evidence rating.
requirements: Address schoolwide behavior issues by involving a school improvement team
Collect information on the hot spots throughout the school, including frequency and timing of particular schoolwide behavior problems
Monitor implementation and outcomes using an efficient method of data collection and allow ample time for the program to work
constraints: Changes in practices, structures, or programs within schools are unlikely to be implemented, sustained, or effective in the long term without concerted attention to enhancing the fundamental relationships within schools
target_learners: All students in U.S. elementary schools (K-5)
target_learning_goals: Reducing negative and fostering positive social interactions schoolwide
examples: Just as teachers document classroom behavior contexts, school leadership teams can map the behavioral territory of the school and use the information to develop prevention strategies and select schoolwide programs.
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/4

article_title: The Continuous Hint Factory - Providing Hints in Vast and Sparsely Populated Edit Distance Spaces
citation: Benjamin Paaßen, Barbara Hammer, Thomas W. Price, Tiffany Barnes, Sebastian Gross, Niels Pinkwart. (2018). The Continuous Hint Factory - Providing Hints in Vast and Sparsely Populated Edit Distance Spaces. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 10, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org
title: Use bottom-out edit hints because principle-based hints are skipped and edit hints reveal only a small part of the solution
description: The article argues for focusing on edit-based bottom-out hints despite pedagogical concerns. Edit hints "display only a very small part of the solution (a single edit), allowing the student to finish most of the problem themselves", and students who game the system "simply skip through such hints to reach the bottom-out hint", so principle-based hints do not prevent hint abuse. More elaborate hint strategies are often unavailable because expert-crafted hint messages are difficult to apply at scale.
requirements: Edit hints should be judged relevant and interpretable, as a study by Price et al. (2017b) indicates for human tutors
constraints: Revealing the next step deprives students of finding it themselves; the article suggests displaying such hints only as a last resort after principle-based hints
target_learners: students requesting help in intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: continuing independent work after receiving a hint
examples: The article cites Aleven et al. (2016) and Shih et al. (2008) on hint reflection and sense-making
key_sources: Benjamin Paaßen, Barbara Hammer, Thomas W. Price, Tiffany Barnes, Sebastian Gross, Niels Pinkwart. (2018). The Continuous Hint Factory - Providing Hints in Vast and Sparsely Populated Edit Distance Spaces. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 10, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/158

article_title: Encouraging Girls in Math and Science
citation: Halpern, D., Aronson, J., Reimer, N., Simpkins, S., Star, J., and Wentzel, K. (2007). Encouraging Girls in Math and Science (NCER 2007-2003). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncer.ed.gov
title: Explicitly teach students that academic abilities are expandable and improvable through effort
description: Teachers should communicate that math and science abilities can be improved through consistent effort and learning, because students who view abilities as fixed experience decreased confidence and performance when facing setbacks. The guide's evidence summary states that "when students are taught that intelligence and abilities can be increased with hard work, their test scores and their grades improve." Teachers can discuss neuroscience showing brains grow new synaptic connections with practice and remind struggling students that understanding gets easier over time.
requirements: Teachers themselves must examine and modify preconceptions that intelligence and abilities are fixed at birth
Teachers remind students of malleability both when they struggle and when they make progress
constraints: Some adults favor natural-ability explanations for success, making it harder to convince students that effort matters
target_learners: K-12 students, especially girls in math and science
target_learning_goals: Accurate beliefs about the malleability of academic ability
Persistence in the face of difficult math and science material
examples: The panel rated this recommendation Moderate based on two small experimental studies with K-12 students, one experimental study with college students, and supporting correlational research.
key_sources: Halpern, D., Aronson, J., Reimer, N., Simpkins, S., Star, J., and Wentzel, K. (2007). Encouraging Girls in Math and Science (NCER 2007-2003). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/5

article_title: Encouraging Girls in Math and Science
citation: Halpern, D., Aronson, J., Reimer, N., Simpkins, S., Star, J., and Wentzel, K. (2007). Encouraging Girls in Math and Science (NCER 2007-2003). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncer.ed.gov
title: Provide students with prescriptive, informational feedback focusing on strategies, effort, and the learning process
description: Teachers should give feedback that focuses on strategies used, effort expended, and the process of learning — for example identifying gains in strategy use or specific errors — rather than general praise such as "good job" or global intelligence praise. The guide states that "Prescriptive, informational feedback enhances students' beliefs about their abilities, typically improves persistence, and improves performance on tasks." It directs girls' attention to what to change after errors rather than letting them attribute wrong answers to lack of ability.
requirements: Multiple opportunities for students to receive feedback on their performance
Feedback that identifies specific strategies or errors rather than simply whether an answer was correct
constraints: A descriptive study of 58 third-grade mathematics classrooms found the primary form of feedback teachers actually use is general praise, which provides no useful information
target_learners: K-12 students in math and science courses
target_learning_goals: Self-efficacy beliefs about mathematics
Persistence on difficult tasks
Correcting misunderstandings and learning from mistakes
examples: The panel rated this recommendation Moderate based on small randomized experimental studies of children performing math or math-related tasks plus supporting research across many designs.
key_sources: Halpern, D., Aronson, J., Reimer, N., Simpkins, S., Star, J., and Wentzel, K. (2007). Encouraging Girls in Math and Science (NCER 2007-2003). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/5

article_title: Using Auxiliary Data to Boost Precision in the Analysis of A/B Tests on an Online Educational Platform
citation: Adam C. Sales, Ethan B. Prihar, Johann A. Gagnon-Bartsch, Neil T. Heffernan. (2023). Using Auxiliary Data to Boost Precision in the Analysis of A/B Tests on an Online Educational Platform: New Data and New Results. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 15, No 2. https://osf.io/k8ph9/
title: When analyzing A/B tests on online learning platforms, use remnant-trained imputation models for covariate adjustment alongside within-sample covariates to gain precision without sacrificing unbiasedness
description: This principle directs platform researchers analyzing randomized experiments to train outcome-prediction models on log data from non-experimental ('remnant') users and incorporate those predictions, together with within-sample covariates, into design-based covariate-adjusted estimators such as ReLOOP+. The article's summary of its findings: "covariate adjustment can lead to substantial gains in precision, with the greatest improvement resulting from adjustment using both within-sample aggregated covariates and remnant-based imputations." Because adjustment is design-based, estimates remain unbiased and inference valid even if the imputation model is poor.
requirements: Access to covariate and outcome log data from users outside the experiment (the remnant)
Randomized treatment assignment so design-based unbiasedness holds
constraints: Gains are smaller when within-sample adjustment alone already performs well; the article reports very rare cases where remnant use reduced precision
target_learners: students in online learning platforms undergoing A/B tests
target_learning_goals: precise, unbiased estimation of causal effects of educational interventions
examples: The article compared T-Test, LOOP, ReLOOP, and ReLOOP+ across 227 randomized ASSISTments contrasts and found remnant-based estimators consistently outperformed those using only within-sample covariate adjustment
key_sources: Adam C. Sales, Ethan B. Prihar, Johann A. Gagnon-Bartsch, Neil T. Heffernan. (2023). Using Auxiliary Data to Boost Precision in the Analysis of A/B Tests on an Online Educational Platform: New Data and New Results. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 15, No 2. https://osf.io/k8ph9/

article_title: Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades
citation: Gersten, R., Baker, S.K., Shanahan, T., Linan-Thompson, S., Collins, P., & Scarcella, R. (2007). Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades: A Practice Guide (NCEE 2007-4011). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Provide focused, intensive small-group reading interventions including the five core reading elements, delivered mainly through explicit, direct instruction
description: The guide recommends intensive small-group interventions for English learners determined to be at risk for reading problems, with time and intensity matched to degree of risk. Interventions "should include the five core reading elements (phonological awareness, phonics, reading fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension)", with "Explicit, direct instruction should be the primary means of instructional delivery." Implementation should be daily for at least 30 minutes in homogeneous groups of three to six students, with training and ongoing support for teachers and interventionists.
requirements: Implemented daily for at least 30 minutes in small, homogeneous groups of three to six students
Training and ongoing support for the teachers and interventionists who provide the small-group instruction
constraints: Amount of time and intensity should reflect the degree of risk determined by reading assessment data and other indicators
target_learners: English learners in the elementary grades at risk for reading problems
target_learning_goals: Foundational reading skills: phonological awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension
examples: Use an intervention program with students who enter the first grade with weak reading and prereading skills, or with older elementary students with reading problems.
key_sources: Gersten, R., Baker, S.K., Shanahan, T., Linan-Thompson, S., Collins, P., & Scarcella, R. (2007). Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades: A Practice Guide (NCEE 2007-4011). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/6

article_title: Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades
citation: Gersten, R., Baker, S.K., Shanahan, T., Linan-Thompson, S., Collins, P., & Scarcella, R. (2007). Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades: A Practice Guide (NCEE 2007-4011). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Provide high-quality vocabulary instruction throughout the day, teaching essential content words in depth and addressing common words, phrases, and expressions not yet learned
description: The guide recommends vocabulary instruction throughout the school day for English learners, graded Strong. Teachers should "Teach essential content words in depth" and also "use instructional time to address the meanings of common words, phrases, and expressions not yet learned." The checklist adds adopting an evidence-based vocabulary approach, developing districtwide lists of essential words drawn from the core reading program and content-area textbooks, and emphasizing everyday words native speakers know that are not necessarily part of the academic curriculum.
requirements: Adopt an evidence-based approach to vocabulary instruction
Develop districtwide lists of essential words drawn from the core reading program and key content-area textbooks
target_learners: English learners in the elementary grades
target_learning_goals: Word meanings, including essential academic content words and everyday words, phrases, and expressions
examples: Districts develop essential-word lists from the core reading program and from textbooks in science and history.

Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/6

article_title: Developing a Feedback Taxonomy for Math: A Synergy of Perspectives through Data Mining Methods
citation: Seiyon M. Lee, Sami Baral, Hongming Chip Li, Li Cheng, Shan Zhang, Carly S. Thorp, Jennifer St. John, Tamisha Thompson, Neil Heffernan, Anthony F. Botelho. (2025). Developing Feedback Taxonomy for Math: A Synergy of Perspectives through Data Mining Methods. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 17, No 2. https://osf.io/puhyr/?view_only=514d8534e9be41d9a57ad82e9efb3249
title: Use an empirically grounded feedback taxonomy as a shared language when designing scalable feedback systems
description: This principle holds that systems generating or supporting feedback — human or AI-driven — should be organized around a taxonomy grounded in authentic classroom practice and co-developed by researchers and practitioners. The article argues that when integrated into learning systems, the taxonomy can support feedback that is "not only pedagogically meaningful but also more consistent, thereby reducing the variability often associated with human-authored feedback at scale." It further recommends using the identified types to guide LLM-based feedback generation and evaluation.
requirements: Taxonomy categories must be grounded in empirical analysis of authentic feedback data rather than derived solely from theory
Coding and framework development should include both researchers and practitioners as coders to account for varying interpretations
constraints: The article notes existing automated systems "often lack frameworks grounded in human-in-the-loop design principles, which limits their interpretability and pedagogical relevance"
The taxonomy was developed only for middle school mathematics teacher feedback
target_learners: K-12 mathematics students receiving feedback through digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: delivering timely, pedagogically grounded, and consistent feedback on open-ended student work at scale
examples: The article states the identified feedback types "may be used to guide prompt engineering, fine-tuning objectives, or evaluation criteria" for LLM-based feedback systems.
key_sources: Seiyon M. Lee, Sami Baral, Hongming Chip Li, Li Cheng, Shan Zhang, Carly S. Thorp, Jennifer St. John, Tamisha Thompson, Neil Heffernan, Anthony F. Botelho. (2025). article_title: Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools
citation: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Signal the need for dramatic change with strong leadership
description: In a failing school, the leader should make a clear commitment to dramatic changes from the status quo and signal the magnitude and urgency of those changes. The guide states that "Leadership is key, but it alone is not adequate" and that the leader must show dramatic changes are necessary. Leaders signal change by communicating a clear purpose, creating high expectations, sharing leadership, and eliminating distractions so classroom time focuses on instruction.
requirements: A change in leadership practices is essential: either install a new principal or have the existing leader radically alter leadership practices
constraints: Strong turnaround leadership sometimes met resistance, including calls from parents for leaders to resign
target_learners: students in chronically low-performing K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: raising student achievement in mathematics and reading within one to three years
examples: New principals entered schools with a clear purpose, set expectations from the first day, and spent long hours studying the school before making immediate changes; one principal led an aggressive community campaign to change the school's perception
key_sources: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/7

article_title: Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools
citation: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Maintain a consistent focus on improving instruction throughout the turnaround
description: Turnaround schools should use data to set goals for instructional improvement, make changes that immediately and directly affect instruction, and continually reassess student learning and instructional practices to refocus goals. The guide reports that "All schools in the case studies focused on improving teaching and student learning by analyzing student assessment and classroom data" and by regularly monitoring progress and adjusting strategies.
requirements: Examine school-level, classroom-level, and student-level data; establish priority instructional areas; provide targeted professional development; and conduct a collaborative curriculum review aligned with state standards
constraints: In one case study of 10 schools, 8 realized they did not have access to sufficient data on student achievement to guide decision-making
target_learners: students in chronically low-performing K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: improving teaching quality and student achievement in targeted subject areas
examples: Schools disaggregated performance data by grade level and learning objectives to identify students needing help on specific skills; principals spent as much as 40 percent of their time in classrooms observing teaching
key_sources: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/7

article_title: Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools
citation: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Make visible improvements early in the turnaround process (quick wins)
description: Early in a turnaround, the school should pursue a goal that is important, achievable quickly, and visibly improved, because quick wins "can rally staff around the effort and overcome resistance and inertia." The strategy should be implementable quickly, for example when the school already has the authority and resources to act.
requirements: Start with a goal that is important, can be achieved quickly, and will provide visible improvement, with a strategy the school can implement quickly
constraints: Signaling change without following through with quick wins could make school staff skeptical
target_learners: students and staff in chronically low-performing K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: building staff commitment and momentum for schoolwide improvement
examples: Common quick-win goals named in the guide include changing the school's use of time, improving access to resources and physical facilities, and improving discipline
key_sources: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). article_title: Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools
citation: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Build a committed staff qualified to carry out school improvement
description: The school leader must build a staff committed to the improvement goals and qualified to carry them out, which "may require changes in staff, such as releasing, replacing, or redeploying staff who are not fully committed." The guide advises assessing staff strengths and weaknesses and recruiting specialists such as interventionists, reading specialists, and instructional coaches.
requirements: Assess staff strengths and weaknesses; redeploy staff with valuable skills but ineffective current roles; replace staff who actively resist turnaround efforts; recruit new staff with needed specialized skills
target_learners: students in chronically low-performing K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: ensuring instruction is delivered by committed, qualified staff
examples: The checklist recommends redeploying staff members who have valuable skills but are not effective in their current role and replacing staff who actively resist the turnaround

article_title: Improving Adolescent Literacy: Effective Classroom and Intervention Practices
citation: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Provide explicit vocabulary instruction in reading, language arts, and content-area classes
description: The guide's first recommendation is that teachers "provide students with explicit vocabulary instruction both as part of reading and language arts classes and as part of content-area classes such as science and social studies." It spans two complementary approaches: direct instruction in word meaning (definitions, semantic maps, recitation) and strategies for independent word learning (semantic, syntactic, and context clues). Implementation steps include dedicating lesson time, repeated exposure in multiple contexts, varied use through discussion and writing, and teaching word-analysis strategies.
requirements: Dedicate a portion of regular classroom lessons to explicit vocabulary instruction
Provide repeated exposure to new words in multiple contexts with sufficient practice sessions
Give opportunities to use new vocabulary through discussion, writing, and extended reading
Teach strategies that make students independent vocabulary learners
constraints: Only some studies show effects on standardized reading comprehension measures; the panel states additional research is needed on that relationship
Words appearing only once or twice in a text are typically not targets for explicit instruction
target_learners: Upper elementary, middle, and high school students, including struggling readers
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of academic and content-area vocabulary
Independent word-learning skills
examples: The panel rates the evidence strong based on six randomized controlled experimental studies and three well designed quasi-experiments demonstrating group equivalence at pretest, plus a single subject design study.

citation: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). title: Provide direct and explicit comprehension strategy instruction with modeling, guided practice, and independent practice
description: The guide's second recommendation is direct and explicit teaching of comprehension strategies such as summarizing, questioning, paraphrasing, and finding the main idea. "Direct and explicit teaching involves a teacher modeling and providing explanations of the specific strategies students are learning, giving guided practice and feedback on the use of the strategies, and promoting independent practice to apply the strategies." Teachers should select appropriate texts, use a direct and explicit lesson plan, adjust guided practice to strategy difficulty, and talk about strategies while teaching them.
requirements: Use a direct and explicit instruction lesson plan for teaching comprehension strategies
Select texts appropriate to students' reading level and to the strategy being taught
Provide the appropriate amount of guided practice depending on strategy difficulty
Show students how to apply strategies to different texts
constraints: Studies compared strategies against business-as-usual controls, so no strategy can be ranked as more powerful than another
target_learners: Upper elementary, middle, and high school students, especially passive readers
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of narrative and content-area texts
examples: The panel rates the evidence strong based on five randomized experimental studies plus a single subject design study of main idea summarization.

title: Provide opportunities for extended discussion of text meaning and interpretation
description: The guide's third recommendation calls for structured, extended small- and large-group discussion of what texts mean and how they should be interpreted. "There is evidence that encouraging high-quality discussion about texts, even in the absence of explicit instruction in reading comprehension strategies, can have a positive impact on reading comprehension skills." Discussion also gives teachers a window into students' thinking that can inform future instruction. Implementation includes preparing engaging materials and questions, using follow-up questions, and developing a specific discussion protocol for small groups.
requirements: Carefully prepare by selecting engaging materials and developing stimulating questions
Ask follow-up questions that provide continuity and extend the discussion
Provide a task or discussion format students can follow in small groups
Develop and practice the use of a specific discussion protocol
constraints: The evidence base is rated moderate rather than strong by the panel
target_learners: Upper elementary, middle, and high school students in content-area classes
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and interpretation of texts
examples: The guide notes one study in which discussion improved knowledge of word meanings and relationships for students reading biology texts.

title: Increase student motivation and engagement in literacy learning through autonomy, relevance, and goal setting
description: The guide's fourth recommendation ties motivation and engagement specifically to literacy outcomes. Teachers should establish meaningful content learning goals, promote autonomy, make literacy experiences relevant to interests and current events, and "build classroom conditions to promote higher reading engagement and conceptual learning through such strategies as goal setting, self-directed learning, and collaborative learning." The panel rates the evidence moderate because motivation and engagement are recognized moderators of learning but the direct link to reading achievement is thinly studied.
requirements: Establish meaningful and engaging content learning goals around the essential ideas of a discipline and the learning processes used to access them
Provide a positive learning environment that promotes student autonomy in learning
Make literacy experiences more relevant to student interests, everyday life, or important current events
Build classroom conditions promoting higher reading engagement through goal setting, self-directed learning, and collaborative learning
constraints: There is limited scientific evidence that links motivation and engagement factors directly to student achievement in reading
target_learners: Upper elementary, middle, and high school students in content-area classes
target_learning_goals: Reading engagement, motivation, and conceptual learning in literacy
examples: The checklist for this recommendation pairs content learning goals around essential disciplinary ideas with autonomy-supportive environments and relevance to student interests and current events.

title: Make available intensive and individualized interventions for struggling readers provided by trained specialists
description: The guide's fifth recommendation addresses students who score well below peers and cannot improve under normal classroom conditions. If struggling readers are identified and "their weaknesses in reading are carefully assessed by trained specialists using measures that detect strengths and weaknesses, and this assessment is followed by intensive interventions that are focused on their particular needs, they will have more opportunities to improve their literacy skills substantially." Intervention intensity should match instructional need, varying with group size and instructional time.
requirements: Use reliable screening assessments to identify students with reading difficulties, followed by formal and informal assessments to pinpoint instructional needs
Select an intervention that provides an explicit instructional focus to meet each student's identified learning needs
Match intervention intensity to student need, relating group size and amount of instructional time to the level of need
constraints: The fifth recommendation refers to reading interventions that in many cases must be provided by reading specialists or specially trained teachers, not ordinary classroom teachers
target_learners: Adolescent struggling readers whose poor literacy skills weaken their ability to make sense of written material
target_learning_goals: Accelerated reading growth toward grade-level literacy standards
examples: The panel rates the evidence strong and warns that schools housing such programs within special education serve only a small proportion of the students who could benefit.

title: Align the OST program academically with the school day
description: OST programs and schools share the mission of helping students succeed, and the panel holds that "academic alignment with the school day is necessary for OST programs to improve academic performance." Alignment is achieved through OST program coordinators and designated school-based coordinators who maintain ongoing communication, align OST activities with state and local content standards and the school curriculum, and coordinate staffing. Tools include a logbook carried between classroom teachers and OST instructors sharing homework assignments, topics covered, and useful instructional strategies.
requirements: An OST program coordinator who maintains regular communication with school staff
A designated school staff person to coordinate communication with OST programs
Identification of school-based goals and learning objectives to connect OST instruction to school instruction
constraints: The level of evidence for this recommendation is low; no study tested its effectiveness individually, only in combination with other OST program components
target_learners: elementary and middle school students in school-based OST programs in low-income, high-needs communities
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in school-day content areas
examples: Coordinators can develop a logbook students carry back and forth daily to share information about OST activities with classroom teachers, and arrange for OST instructors to periodically attend common planning periods with classroom teachers.

title: Maximize student participation and attendance in OST programs
description: Because students most likely to benefit from a strong academic program may be especially unlikely to enroll in or attend OST programs regularly, the panel recommends that "OST programs focus on recruiting and retaining targeted students so that they receive the dosage necessary to realize academic benefits." Program features should be designed to meet the needs and preferences of students and parents, awareness of the program should be promoted within schools and to parents, and attendance data should be used to identify students facing difficulties attending.

Promotion of program awareness within schools and to parents
Use of attendance data to identify students facing attendance difficulties
constraints: The level of evidence for this recommendation is low
target_learners: elementary and middle school students targeted for academic assistance in OST programs
target_learning_goals: sustained attendance sufficient to receive the instructional dosage needed for academic benefits
examples: The checklist for this recommendation lists designing program features to meet needs and preferences, promoting awareness, and using attendance data to identify students facing difficulties in attending the program.

title: Adapt OST instruction to individual and small group needs
description: To maximize educational benefits, OST instruction should respond to each student's needs. The recommendation presents "strategies for the structuring of instructional practices and program content to address the needs of students and effectively improve academic outcomes," including organizing instructional time and facilitating individualized teaching by assessing student needs. Action steps are to use formal and informal assessment data to inform academic instruction, use one-on-one tutoring if possible or otherwise break students into small groups, and provide professional development and ongoing instructional support to all instructors.

One-on-one tutoring where possible, otherwise small-group instruction
Professional development and ongoing instructional support for all instructors
target_learners: elementary and middle school OST students with varied academic needs
target_learning_goals: academic outcomes addressed through individualized and small-group instruction
examples: This is the only recommendation the panel rates as having a moderate level of evidence, and it is intended for teachers struggling with addressing the academic needs of their students.

title: Provide engaging learning experiences in OST programs
description: OST programs should capitalize on their programming flexibility by offering activities students find especially engaging, particularly when students may be fatigued after a long school day, on Saturdays, or during summer months. The guide recommends making learning relevant by incorporating practical examples and connecting instruction to student interests and experiences, making learning active through collaborative learning and hands-on academic activities, and building adult-student relationships. To avoid the pitfalls of programs that failed to show academic effects, all activities should have a specific learning objective.

Learning made relevant through practical examples and connections to student interests

Adult-student relationships built among OST participants
constraints: The level of evidence for this recommendation is low

target_learning_goals: engagement in academically oriented OST activities with specific learning objectives
examples: The panel suggests engaging students when they may be fatigued after a long day of school, on Saturdays, or during the summer months, and notes 21st CCLC programs emphasized sports or extracurricular activities because those were thought more popular with students.

title: Assess OST program performance and use results to improve program quality
description: Program improvement depends on articulating goals and expectations, effective management, and staff performance and experience. "Recommendation 5 presents strategies for schools and districts to use to identify programs that are most likely to result in academic improvement and to monitor existing programs to ensure that the highest-quality services are being provided to students." Action steps are to develop an evaluation plan, collect program and student performance data, analyze the data and use findings for program improvement, and conduct a summative evaluation.

citation: The Conceptual Basis for Fractions. (2011). Developed at least in part with Federal funds from the U.S. Department of Education under contract number ED-PEP-11-C-0068. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/
title: Build early fraction concepts on children's informal understanding of sharing and proportionality
description: This principle holds that primary-grade teachers should treat children's everyday knowledge of sharing and proportionality as the foundation for formal fraction instruction. The presentation states that "Young children come to school with an informal understanding of sharing and proportionality" and that teachers "can build on that informal understanding to develop fraction concepts." It frames effective learning as connecting new ideas to what children already understand in real-world contexts.
requirements: Teachers in the primary grades pose sharing problems drawn from familiar real-world contexts
target_learners: primary-grade students (K-2) before formal fraction instruction
target_learning_goals: initial fraction concepts
equal sharing
proportional relationships
examples: A first-grade teacher asks students to divide 12 pretzels equally among four friends, with some children drawing pictures and others counting out pretzels one by one

title: Six-element quality checklist for community engagement session questions
description: A handout adapted from a program evaluation toolkit assesses each drafted session question against six key elements: the question should be 'Pertinent', 'Answerable', 'Reasonable', 'Specific', 'Evaluative', and 'Complete', each with yes/no ratings and notes. title: Assign a single primary advocate to each student who needs intensive, individualized support
description: For students who have fallen off track and face significant challenges, the guide recommends assigning one person as the student's primary advocate who provides intensive monitoring and personalized intervention. The principle states: "For each student identified as needing individualized support, assign a single person to be the student's primary advocate." Advocates draw on a menu of support options and receive ongoing professional learning and tracking tools. This recommendation carries a Moderate Evidence rating from the panel.

Advocates need ongoing professional learning opportunities and tools for tracking their work

description: The panel recommends choosing a single routine that gives students simple, reusable steps for tackling unfamiliar multisyllabic words. "Rather than teaching a wide array of rules, choose a routine that provides simple steps for breaking words into parts and blending those parts together to sound out the word." Teachers explicitly demonstrate the routine, guide students through applying it to several words, and post abbreviated steps or prompt cards so students can apply it independently across different words.

description: Although timed readings are common in fluency work, the panel warns against overreliance on speed. "Timed readings can be overused and can be a detriment to student engagement and motivation, especially when used solely to increase reading speed." Instead, fluency-building activities should also target reading effortlessly with automaticity and reading with expression or prosody, using engaging activities that build confidence.

title: For students who decode well but comprehend poorly, minimize decoding and fluency instruction and maximize comprehension instruction
description: The panel advises differentiating intervention content by profile: students who read multisyllabic words effortlessly but perform poorly on reading tests because of weak vocabulary and comprehension difficulties need language work, not more decoding. "Teachers should minimize decoding and fluency instruction and maximize comprehension instruction." These students should be grouped into interventions focused on oral language and reading comprehension.
requirements: Group these students in an intervention focusing on oral language and reading comprehension
Include activities that increase world knowledge and word knowledge with meaningful discussion of texts

target_learning_goals: Oral language development and reading comprehension
examples: The panel's obstacle advice recommends including words from core subject-area classes during intervention time, such as Reconstruction and suffrage for a Civil War unit

article_title: Leading Early Childhood Achievement and Development (LEAD) Partnership
citation: Leading Early Childhood Achievement and Development (LEAD) Partnership. (2025). Regional Educational Laboratory (REL) partnership logic model.
title: State-level partnership logic model linking leader support to teacher practice change
description: The LEAD logic model exhibits a reusable design pattern: a state education agency partners with a research laboratory to change classroom practice indirectly, by first building school leaders' knowledge so they "Adapt and implement school policies and practices to support use of research-based early learning practices", while teachers simultaneously gain knowledge and increase use of the practices. Leadership support and teacher professional development are treated as parallel, mutually reinforcing strands leading to student outcomes.
requirements: School leaders must be included as professional development recipients, not only teachers
constraints: The pattern assumes leader policy and practice adaptation happens at the medium-term stage, after short-term knowledge gains
target_learners: prekindergarten and kindergarten students
target_learning_goals: literacy and math achievement through improved early learning practices
examples: The logic model assigns short-term knowledge outcomes to both leaders and teachers, a medium-term policy/practice outcome to leaders, and a practice-use outcome to teachers.

title: Teach struggling readers one consistent routine for decoding multisyllabic words
description: Rather than teaching many rules, the panel recommends choosing a single routine with simple steps for breaking words into parts and blending them, then teaching it explicitly through modeling, guided practice, and independent application. The guide states the panel "recommends choosing one routine to teach students during the intervention" and to "choose a routine that provides simple steps for breaking words into parts and blending those parts together to sound out the word." Steps include identifying prefixes and suffixes, underlining vowel sounds, and blending parts into a recognizable word.
requirements: Post abbreviated steps of the routine on the board or provide prompt cards so reminders are readily available
Assess students' word-reading skills before the intervention to place students with similar needs in groups
constraints: Students who have mastered simple and advanced letter combinations do not need a word-reading intervention, though they may still benefit from vocabulary or comprehension remediation

target_learning_goals: Accurately decoding complex multisyllabic words in grade-level texts
examples: Example 1.1 shows a teacher modeling a four-step routine on the word unreasonable, circling the prefix un- and suffix -able, underlining vowel sounds, looping word parts, and blending

title: Give each repeated reading a purpose rather than rereading only for speed
description: Rereading the same passage several times builds fluency, but unstructured rereading can feel dull and discouraging for upper-elementary and middle school students. The guide recommends that "students reread the same passage a total of 3–4 times, each time with a different purpose," such as answering questions, identifying unknown words, or reading with expression, and that teachers briefly discuss responses after each reading to hold students accountable. Purposes can vary with the reading ability of the group.
requirements: Choose short, content-rich passages at students' instructional level that include previously taught words, sounds, or vocabulary
Provide feedback after each reading that affirms correct responses and clarifies misconceptions
constraints: Timed readings should be used with caution because they can be overused and can detrimentally affect engagement and motivation when used solely to increase speed
target_learners: Students in grades 4-9 with reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Reading text effortlessly and with understanding
examples: Example 2.2 shows a small group reading a paragraph on poverty and feeding a family, first silently explaining it to a partner, then reading aloud in turns to answer board questions

article_title: Teaching Math to Young Children
citation: Frye, D., Baroody, A. J., Burchinal, M., Carver, S. M., Jordan, N. C., & McDowell, J. (2013). Teaching math to young children: A practice guide (NCEE 2014-4005). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Teach number and operations using a developmental progression, starting with subitizing small collections
description: The guide's first recommendation establishes number and operations as the foundational early math content area and prescribes an ordered sequence: "First, provide opportunities for children to practice recognizing the total number of objects in small collections (one to three items) and labeling them with a number word without needing to count them." Teachers then promote one-to-one counting, counting-based comparison of quantities, labeling collections with number words and numerals, and finally solving basic problems, moving from small to progressively larger collections at each step.
requirements: Instruction must build on the knowledge children already possess and identify the next developmental step
Children should first work with small collections of one to three objects before moving to larger collections
constraints: The evidence supports number and operations instruction generally, not any particular developmental progression
target_learners: children ages 3 to 6 in preschool, prekindergarten, and kindergarten
target_learning_goals: subitizing
one-to-one counting and cardinality
comparing quantities
basic arithmetic problems
examples: The Basic Hiding game practices subitizing by covering one to three objects and asking children how many are hidden; snack-time and transition moments are used for quick "How many?" practice.
key_sources: Frye, D., Baroody, A. J., Burchinal, M., Carver, S. M., Jordan, N. C., & McDowell, J. (2013). Teaching math to young children: A practice guide (NCEE 2014-4005). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Teach geometry, patterns, measurement, and data analysis using a developmental progression alongside number
description: The guide's second recommendation extends developmental-progression teaching beyond number to four other content areas. It advises: "Help children to recognize, name, and compare shapes, and then teach them to combine and separate shapes," and similarly to have children identify then extend, correct, and create patterns, make direct comparisons and use informal and formal measurement units, and collect, organize, and graphically represent information. The panel argues early experience in these areas prepares children for later subjects such as algebra and statistics.
requirements: Material in each content area must be organized according to a developmental progression
constraints: This recommendation received a minimal evidence rating; supporting studies combined it with other practices

target_learning_goals: shape recognition, combining and separating
pattern extension and creation
measurement with informal and formal units
collecting, organizing, and graphing data
examples: Examples include the Shapes game, creating and extending patterns, a favorites survey represented graphically, and vocabulary tables for types of measurement.

article_title: Intelligent Tutoring for Structure Strategy (ITSS)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, April). Web-based Intelligent Tutoring for the Structure Strategy (ITSS). https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Faded recall sequence within ITSS exercises: scaffolded summaries progress to unsupported recall
description: ITSS exercises follow a recurring multi-step sequence: read nonfiction text, identify the top-level text structure, select signaling words, write a main-idea sentence, generate a thorough summary with comprehension tools, and finally write a recall summary. Scaffolding fades across lessons: "In early lessons, students recall and summarize the text while having access to their (or the I.T.'s) main idea summaries from steps 4 or 5. Later practice lessons remove this aid, and students monitor their recall using the structure strategy." Passages also become more difficult as students complete the exercises.
requirements: The Intelligent Tutor provides feedback after each step; after several unsuccessful attempts it offers hints and a model summary that students may not copy.
constraints: In fourth-grade classrooms in the 2012 study, the recall task was removed after the first month because students had difficulty typing.
target_learners: Students in grades K-8 using ITSS during English language arts
target_learning_goals: Identifying text structure, signaling words, main ideas, and summarizing and recalling factual text
examples: Exercises use passages from science, social studies, sports, and current events; some lessons ask students to write titles, compose their own texts, or correct a fictitious student's muddled use of the strategy.

citation: Baker, S., Geva, E., Kieffer, M. J., Lesaux, N., Linan-Thompson, S., Morris, J., Proctor, C. P., & Russell, R. (2014). Teaching Academic Content and Literacy to English Learners in Elementary and Middle School. What Works Clearinghouse Practice Guide. https://www.whatworks.ed.gov
title: Select a small set of academic vocabulary words for in-depth instruction using explicit selection criteria
description: Rather than teaching every unfamiliar word, educators should choose a small set of academic vocabulary for in-depth instruction. The guide's selection matrix screens candidate words against criteria: whether the word is "Frequently used in the text", "Central to understanding the text", "Appears in other content areas", has useful "Affixes", "Multiple meanings and uses", and "Cross-language potential". In the worked zoo-text example, words like environment, exhibit, impact, investigation, option, and pursuit were screened this way.
requirements: A brief, engaging informational text containing academic vocabulary serves as the platform for the word set
constraints: Schools with strict district-mandated curricula may need to use existing resources and publicly available complex texts
target_learners: English learners in elementary and middle school (K-8)
target_learning_goals: Academic vocabulary knowledge supporting content-area comprehension
examples: The guide's Step 2 matrix screens six candidate words from a zoo-design informational text against the six criteria

title: Provide scaffolded small-group instruction with frequent practice and review of newly learned skills across varied contexts over several lessons
description: Small-group intervention for struggling students should be scaffolded so that students get "frequent opportunities for students to practice and review newly learned skills and concepts in various contexts over several lessons to ensure retention." The guide also advises that for students struggling with basic foundational reading skills, time should go not only to those skills but also to vocabulary development and listening and reading comprehension strategies, illustrated with a teacher think-aloud modeling inferential comprehension of a Rosa Parks text.
requirements: Use assessment information to identify students with persistent struggles and design intervention content targeting identified needs
constraints: One-size-fits-all interventions are unlikely to meet diverse needs of English learners who struggle; keep a portfolio of intervention options
When a majority of English learners struggle with a grade-level comprehension skill, teach it in core classroom instruction rather than delegating it to Tier 2

article_title: Teaching Strategies for Improving Algebra Knowledge in Middle and High School Students
citation: Star, J. R., Caronongan, P., Foegen, A., Furgeson, J., Keating, B., Larson, M. R., Lyskawa, J., McCallum, W. G., Porath, J., & Zbiek, R. M. (2015). Teaching strategies for improving algebra knowledge in middle and high school students (NCEE 2015-4010). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Use solved problems to engage students in analyzing algebraic reasoning and strategies
description: This recommendation has teachers present worked examples showing both the problem and the solution steps, and have students discuss and analyze the structures, steps, and reasoning rather than only producing answers. The rationale is that "Solved problems can minimize the burden of abstract reasoning by allowing students to see the problem and many solution steps at once—without executing each step—helping students learn more efficiently." Implementation steps include discussing solved problem structures, selecting problems matched to the lesson's aim including common errors, and using whole-class discussion, small-group work, and independent practice with incomplete or alternating solved problems.
requirements: Solved problems should reflect the lesson's instructional aim, and incorrect solved problems must be clearly labeled so students do not confuse correct and incorrect strategies
constraints: The guide rates the supporting evidence Minimal; the studies meeting WWC standards did not examine solved problems across different situations, so broader use rests on panel belief
target_learners: Students in remedial, regular, and honors algebra classes in grades 6-12
target_learning_goals: Analyzing algebraic reasoning and solution strategies
Developing deeper understanding of solution processes
examples: Teachers present parallel correct and incorrect solved problems for factoring and completing the square, with probing questions guiding discussion of strategic and procedural errors
Independent practice alternates a solved problem with a similar unsolved problem so students use the worked example to guide their own work

Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Teach students to utilize the structure of algebraic representations
description: This recommendation directs teachers to make the underlying mathematical features and relationships of expressions, equations, and graphs explicit through precise mathematical language, reflective questioning, and comparison of alternative representations. The guide states that "Paying attention to structure helps students make connections among problems, solution strategies, and representations that may initially appear different but are actually mathematically similar." Steps include promoting language that reflects mathematical structure, encouraging reflective questioning while solving, and teaching that different forms of the same equation convey different information.
requirements: Teachers model precise mathematical language and rephrase vague student language, since no WWC-standard study examines the precise-language component and the panel bases it on expert judgment
constraints: The guide rates the evidence Minimal; the language component specifically has no supporting WWC-standard study
target_learners: Students learning algebra in grades 6-12, including students with specific learning challenges
target_learning_goals: Recognizing structure in algebraic representations
Using precise mathematical language
Comparing multiple representations of the same relationship
examples: Students compare slope-intercept and point-slope forms of the same line to see what each form reveals easily
A reflective-questioning poster lists questions such as asking what relationships exist between quantities in an expression

article_title: engage2learn
citation: engage2learn (e2L): Evidence Rating. (2022). https://www.evidenceforlearning.org
title: Partner districts with coaching providers that customize job-embedded professional learning to district priorities and align educator growth with learner outcomes
description: The article's program model is that e2L "partners with public schools to provide competency-focused, evidence-based coaching and job-embedded support for educators and administrators", customizing "to each partner district's specific needs and priorities". Professional learning is used to align educator growth with learner outcomes directly, rather than delivering generic training. The two matched studies linking e2L coaching to student achievement gains support this principle at a moderate evidence level.
requirements: District partnership to identify specific needs and priorities
Job-embedded coaching rather than standalone workshops
constraints: Evidence comes from two matched studies in 6th-8th grade settings in a large urban Texas district; the summary reports conflicting STAAR results in the first study
target_learners: educators and administrators in partner public school districts
target_learning_goals: improving instructional quality
improving student achievement outcomes
examples: e2L partnered with a large urban Texas district to coach 169 teachers across 10 schools during 2021-2022, and ran a second propensity-score-matched study with a second cohort of e2L teachers.

article_title: Using Technology to Support Postsecondary Student Learning
citation: Dabbagh, N., Bass, R., Bishop, M., Costelloe, S., Cummings, K., Freeman, B., Frye, M., Picciano, A. G., Porowski, A., Sparrow, J., & Wilson, S. J. (2019). Washington, DC: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Use communication and collaboration tools to increase interaction among students and between students and instructors
description: The guide recommends that postsecondary instructors and administrators use communication and collaboration tools—synchronous, asynchronous, and social networking—to increase engagement by letting students communicate about course content and learning experiences. It states that relationships formed with instructors and peers "enable them to create connections around common learning goals, build knowledge and identity, and develop a sense of belonging." Implementation steps include selecting tools aligned to learning objectives, considering student preferences and access, articulating expectations, monitoring participation, and assessing what is working.
requirements: Select tools that best support the course's learning objectives
Articulate expectations for when and how students should use the tools, with shared grading criteria and rubrics
Monitor student participation and provide facilitation and feedback as needed
constraints: The panel assigned a minimal level of evidence based on three studies, only one of which meets WWC group design standards without reservations
Privacy concerns may discourage use; instructors should allow concerned students to opt out
target_learners: postsecondary students at 2- and 4-year colleges and universities
target_learning_goals: student engagement, sense of belonging, and persistence through interaction around course content
examples: Schools App, a social networking tool with a study group finder, group and private messaging, and institutional announcements

title: Use varied, personalized, and readily available digital resources to design and deliver instructional content
description: The guide recommends leveraging technology to vary, blend, or accelerate course formats and to package course content to minimize cost, maximize accessibility, and accommodate different learning preferences. It argues that formats requiring students "to be in a specific place, at a specific time, and for a fixed duration necessarily bound opportunities for interaction." Blended and flipped formats can preserve class time for hands-on activities, group assignments, and individualized instruction, and interactive modules can provide immediate feedback through adaptive learning features.

Use design frameworks such as ADDIE to develop flexible delivery formats aligned with course goals
constraints: Rated moderate evidence based on 16 studies (eleven meeting WWC standards without reservations, five with reservations)
Planning online education requires attention to institutional context, available finances, and hardware and software

target_learning_goals: deeper engagement with course content and flexible access to learning materials
examples: The Open Learning Initiative (OLI) Statistics course in an accelerated blended format, and Time Compressed Animated Delivery (TCAD) of follicular dynamics in reproductive physiology

title: Use technology to provide timely and targeted feedback on student performance
description: The guide recommends using technology to provide timely and targeted feedback on student performance, including classroom polling tools, classroom response systems, and varied question types for clicker questions. Feedback technologies let instructors gauge understanding during class and respond to student performance quickly, supporting learning in face-to-face, blended, and online settings.

citation: Digital Promise, The Jim Henson Company, Concord Evaluation Group, & Curious Media. (2021). Designing an app to support families' joint engagement with media: Design principles and lessons from research. [White Paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/121
title: Provide clear instructions for alternative ways to access content when including features like automatic sync
description: This principle holds that a second-screen app should pair an automatic content recognition sync feature with clear instructions for other ways families can access content, because some families cannot or prefer not to use sync. The team recommends incorporating sync since many who used it found it valuable, while noting "it would also be necessary to provide multiple ways to access information in the app."
requirements: The app includes a sync feature that many families find valuable for accessing episode-related content
constraints: Some families cannot use sync because they watch episodes and use the app on the same device rather than accessing the app on a second device
37.5% of families that did not use sync indicated technical difficulties or issues figuring out how to use the feature
target_learners: Parents and caregivers of young children
target_learning_goals: Supporting children's science learning through joint media engagement
examples: The team moved the icon that launched the sync feature to make navigation more intuitive and added a pop-up reminding families to try again after the theme song was complete

title: Include conversation starters to help families discuss key ideas while watching and reflect after viewing
description: This principle recommends embedding conversation starters in family media apps to encourage discussion of key science ideas during viewing and reflection afterward. Findings from Phases 3 and 4 showed families "accessed and used all different sets of conversation starters to engage in science talk," and parents reported feeling more confident engaging in science talk after using the app.
requirements: Prompts designed for before, during, and after viewing scenarios
Prompts aligned to families' typical co-viewing interaction patterns
constraints: Families did not necessarily use the starters as initially designed; some used before and during prompts after viewing because they did not want to interrupt children
Before prompts were most challenging because families did not have context for the episode

target_learning_goals: Facilitating rich science conversations between parents and children

title: Collaboratively designed inventory checklist for comparing existing edtech tools
description: A reusable checklist pattern in which cross-team stakeholders compare multiple products intended to accomplish the same impact across shared criteria. The report's sample checklist rows include per-student cost, instructional goal, hardware compatibility, login requirements, educator and student review, curricular and state-standards alignment, Research-Based Design and Learner Variability certification status, and customer support responsiveness.
